questions.q: What is layering? Why is layering useful in computer networking?
questions.a:
Layering means dividing networking into separate levels, where each layer has it’s own job. 
It is useful because:
Each layer can work somewhat independently
You can change one layer without redesigning everything.
It makes networks easier to understand and troubleshoot.
Divides one complicated network process into smaller jobs.
questions.practiceQ: What is layering? Why is layering useful in computer networking?
questions.explain: Each layer hides details from the layer above it. For example, an application can keep using IP even if the local connection changes from copper Ethernet to Wi-Fi. This separation also lets you troubleshoot one responsibility at a time.
questions.quizAnswer: Separate responsibilities into layers so parts can change independently and troubleshooting is easier.
distractors: Repeat the same job at every layer so all layers must be redesigned together.
Put all networking functions in one layer so no interfaces are needed.
Separate devices by manufacturer so each vendor uses an unrelated network process.
questions.remember: Remember: Layering splits one large networking task into smaller jobs. Changing one job does not require redesigning everything.

questions.q: What are the layers of the TCP/ IP stack?
questions.a:
Top to bottom:
Application -> Transport -> Network/IP -> Data Link -> Physical
Application: What am I sending?
Transport: How should it be delivered?
Network: Where is it going?
Data Link: How do I reach the next device?
Physical: How do the actual bits travel?
questions.practiceQ: What are the layers of the TCP/ IP stack?
questions.explain: Read the stack from the user toward the wire: the application creates data, transport connects processes, IP routes packets, the data-link layer delivers frames locally, and the physical layer carries the bits.
questions.quizAnswer: Application → Transport → Network/IP → Data Link → Physical
distractors: Application → Network/IP → Transport → Data Link → Physical
Application → Transport → Data Link → Network/IP → Physical
Physical → Transport → Network/IP → Data Link → Application
questions.remember: Remember: Start at the application and move toward the wire: Application, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.

questions.q: What are the primary functions of each layer in the TCP/ IP stack?
questions.a:
Application: Provides network services to applications/users
Transport: End-to-end communication between applications
Network/IP: IP addressing and routing
Data Link: Transfers frames on the local network; uses MAC addresses
Physical: Sends bits as electrical/light/radio signals
IP address: Network layer
MAC address: Data Link layer
questions.practiceQ: What are the primary functions of each layer in the TCP/ IP stack?
questions.explain:
Each TCP/IP layer has a different responsibility.
Application: provides network services to applications.
Transport: connects application processes end to end.
Network: uses IP addresses to route packets between networks.
Data Link: transfers frames over a local link using MAC addresses.
Physical: transmits bits as signals.
questions.quizAnswer: Application: services; Transport: end-to-end processes; Network: IP routing; Data Link: local frames/MAC; Physical: signals.
distractors: Application: services; Transport: IP routing; Network: end-to-end processes; Data Link: local frames/MAC; Physical: signals.
Application: signals; Transport: end-to-end processes; Network: IP routing; Data Link: local frames/MAC; Physical: services.
Application: services; Transport: end-to-end processes; Network: local MAC frames; Data Link: IP routing; Physical: signals.
questions.remember: Remember: Keep the delivery scopes separate: Transport connects processes, Network routes between networks, and Data Link delivers on a local link.

questions.q: What is the Open Standards Interconnect (OSI) model? What was the motivation for the development of the OSI model?
questions.a: OSI means Open Systems Interconnection. It is a seven-layer reference model intended to standardize network functions and enable interoperability between different vendors.
questions.practiceQ: What is the Open Standards Interconnect (OSI) model? What was the motivation for the development of the OSI model?
questions.explain: The key idea is interoperability: a common reference model lets different vendors describe the same networking functions. OSI expands to Open Systems Interconnection, rather than the wording in the original prompt.
questions.quizAnswer: Open Systems Interconnection: a seven-layer reference model supporting standardization and interoperability.
distractors: Open Systems Interconnection: a five-layer model created to eliminate interoperability.
Open Systems Interconnection: a seven-layer model requiring all equipment from one vendor.
Open Systems Interconnection: a seven-layer model intended only to describe cable construction.
questions.remember: Remember: OSI means Open Systems Interconnection. It gives different vendors a common seven-layer reference.

questions.q: What are the seven layers of the OSI model? What are the primary functions of each of the seven layers of the OSI model?
questions.a:
From top to bottom:
Application: Network services for application
Presentation: Formats, encrypts, compresses data
Session: Starts, manages, ends communication sessions
Transport: End-to end delivery
Network: IP addressing and routing
Data Link: Frames and MAC addresses
Physical: Sends bits/signals
Mnemonic: APSTNDP - All people seem to need data processing
questions.practiceQ: What are the seven layers of the OSI model? What are the primary functions of each of the seven layers of the OSI model?
questions.explain: The top three OSI layers separate application services, data representation and session management. The bottom four handle end-to-end delivery, routing, local frames and actual signals. Remember APSTNDP from top to bottom.
questions.quizAnswer: Application → Presentation → Session → Transport → Network → Data Link → Physical; representation belongs to Presentation and session management to Session.
distractors: Application → Session → Presentation → Transport → Network → Data Link → Physical; representation belongs to Session.
Application → Presentation → Session → Network → Transport → Data Link → Physical; routing belongs to Transport.
Application → Presentation → Session → Transport → Data Link → Network → Physical; MAC frames belong to Network.
questions.remember: Remember: The top three OSI layers are Application, Presentation and Session. The bottom four are Transport, Network, Data Link and Physical.

questions.q: What are the computer network authorities?
questions.a:
These are organizations responsible for networking standards and internet resources
IEEE -> LAN/WLAN standards, such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi
IETF -> Internet standards such as TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP
questions.practiceQ: What are the computer network authorities?
questions.explain: Associate IEEE with the local link (Ethernet and Wi-Fi) and IETF with Internet protocols (such as TCP/IP and DNS). Standards organizations define shared rules so products can communicate.
questions.quizAnswer: IEEE develops LAN/WLAN standards; IETF develops Internet protocol standards.
distractors: IEEE develops Internet protocols; IETF develops LAN/WLAN standards.
IEEE and IETF primarily allocate regional IP-address blocks rather than develop standards.
IEEE and IETF both define only physical cable dimensions, not communication standards.
questions.remember: Remember: IEEE covers LAN/WLAN standards such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi. IETF covers Internet protocols such as TCP/IP and DNS.

questions.q: What is the primary responsibility of the physical layer in data communication?
questions.a:
The Physical Layer transmits raw bits (0s and 1s) through a physical medium using signals.
Bits -> Signals -> Travel through medium
questions.practiceQ: What is the primary responsibility of the physical layer in data communication?
questions.explain: Bits are abstract values. The physical layer represents those values as a measurable electrical voltage, light pulse or radio signal that can travel through a medium.
questions.quizAnswer: Transmit raw bits through a medium as physical signals.
distractors: Route IP packets between networks using logical addresses.
Form local frames and interpret their source/destination MAC addresses.
Provide end-to-end communication between application processes.
questions.remember: Remember: A 0 or 1 must be carried by something real: an electrical signal, light or radio. That is the Physical layer’s job.

questions.q: Define physical medium in the context of computer networking. What are the common physical media used in computer networks?
questions.a:
A physical medium is what carries a network signal from one device to another.
Common media:
Copper cable
Fiber-optic cable
Wireless/radio
questions.practiceQ: Define physical medium in the context of computer networking. What are the common physical media used in computer networks?
questions.explain: The medium is the path a signal uses, not the protocol that controls communication. Copper carries electrical signals, fiber carries light, and wireless uses radio waves through space.
questions.quizAnswer: A signal-carrying medium, commonly copper cable, optical fiber or wireless/radio space.
distractors: A logical address that tells the network where a host is located.
A frame format that defines the order of header fields.
A route entry that lists the next router on a path.
questions.remember: Remember: The medium is the path the signal uses. Copper, fiber and the space used by radio are different paths.

questions.q: What properties are required for a material to be suitable for use as a physical medium in computer networks?
questions.a:
It should:
Carry signals effectively
Support high speeds/bandwidth
Work over the needed distance
Resist interference/noise
Be reliable and practical to install
questions.practiceQ: What properties are required for a material to be suitable for use as a physical medium in computer networks?
questions.explain: A medium must work for the particular link. A cable that supports the needed speed over a short distance may not do so over a long distance; noise resistance, installation and reliability also matter.
questions.quizAnswer: Required bandwidth and distance, effective signal transmission, noise resistance, reliability and practicality.
distractors: Maximum bandwidth alone, regardless of distance or interference.
Longest possible distance alone, regardless of data rate or installation needs.
The same appearance as other cables, regardless of signal performance.
questions.remember: Remember: A useful medium must carry the needed speed over the needed distance and cope with interference and installation costs.

questions.q: What is UTP? What factors favor the use of optical fiber as a physical medium over copper? Categories of UTP and their speeds.
questions.a: UTP = Unshielded Twisted Pair. Twists reduce interference. Cat 5e: 1 Gbps to 100 m. Cat 6: 1 Gbps to 100 m; 10 Gbps at shorter runs (often up to 55 m, installation dependent). Cat 6a: 10 Gbps to 100 m. Cat 8: 25/40 Gbps to 30 m; Cat 8 is shielded, not UTP. Fiber is useful for long distance, high bandwidth and immunity to electromagnetic interference.
questions.practiceQ: What is UTP? What factors favor the use of optical fiber as a physical medium over copper? Categories of UTP and their speeds.
questions.explain: Twisting copper pairs helps reduce interference. Fiber carries light, so it is immune to electromagnetic interference and supports longer links with suitable optics. Cable category, speed and maximum channel length must be considered together; Cat 8 is shielded.
questions.quizAnswer: UTP is Unshielded Twisted Pair; fiber favors distance, bandwidth and EMI resistance; Cat 5e ≈ 1 Gbps, Cat 6a ≈ 10 Gbps, Cat 8 ≈ 25–40 Gbps.
distractors: UTP is Unshielded Twisted Pair; fiber is more vulnerable to EMI than copper; Cat 5e ≈ 1 Gbps, Cat 6a ≈ 10 Gbps.
UTP is Unshielded Transmission Pair; Cat 5e ≈ 10 Gbps, Cat 6a ≈ 1 Gbps, Cat 8 ≈ 25–40 Gbps.
UTP is Unshielded Twisted Pair; Cat 6 always supports 10 Gbps at every distance; fiber has no distance advantage.
questions.remember: Remember: UTP means Unshielded Twisted Pair. Fiber carries light and resists electromagnetic interference. Cable speeds depend on category and distance.

questions.q: What is total internal reflection? How does it help optical fiber transmit light signals efficiently?
questions.a:
It is the process that keeps light bouncing inside the fiber’s glass core instead of escaping.
That allows the light to signal to travel long distance efficiently.
Light trapped inside the fiber.
questions.practiceQ: What is total internal reflection? How does it help optical fiber transmit light signals efficiently?
questions.explain: The core has a higher refractive index than its cladding. Above the critical angle, light reflects back into the core rather than escaping, keeping the signal guided along the fiber.
questions.quizAnswer: Light is reflected back within the fiber core instead of escaping, helping it travel along the fiber.
distractors: Light escapes the core into the surroundings at every reflection, which improves transmission.
Light is converted into electrical current each time it reaches the edge of the core.
The fiber absorbs each light pulse completely and replaces it with a radio wave.
questions.remember: Remember: Total internal reflection keeps light guided inside the fiber core instead of letting it escape.

questions.q: What are the two categories of optical fiber? Under what conditions is each category preferred? Their distance covered (and diameters of glass)
questions.a: Single-mode fiber: about 9 μm core, preferred for long distances; kilometer-scale links depend on optics (for example 10GBASE-LR supports 10 km). Multimode: 50 or 62.5 μm core, preferred for shorter building/data-center links; 10GBASE-SR supports 300 m on OM3 or 400 m on OM4. Reach is not one fixed distance per fiber type: it depends on fiber grade, wavelength, transceiver and data rate.
questions.practiceQ: What are the two categories of optical fiber? Under what conditions is each category preferred? Their distance covered (and diameters of glass)
questions.explain: A small single-mode core limits the number of light paths, reducing dispersion over long links. Multimode has a larger core and multiple paths, which can spread pulses out. Reach depends on the fiber grade and optics, not just the word “fiber.”
questions.quizAnswer: Single-mode: about 9 μm core, generally longer links; multimode: larger 50/62.5 μm core, generally shorter links; exact reach depends on optics.
distractors: Single-mode: larger 50/62.5 μm core, generally shorter links; multimode: about 9 μm core, generally longer links.
Single-mode and multimode both have a 9 μm core and identical reach with every transceiver.
Multimode always reaches farther because a larger core guarantees greater distance.
questions.remember: Remember: Single-mode has a small core, about 9 µm. Multimode has a larger 50 or 62.5 µm core. Actual reach depends on the optics.

questions.q: What is the need to convert data to signals?
questions.a:
Because the physical medium cannot directly transmit abstract 0s and 1s.
The data must be represented as physical signal, such as:
Electrical signal
Light
Radio wave
questions.practiceQ: What is the need to convert data to signals?
questions.explain: A receiver cannot sense an abstract number directly. The sender must encode the data into a physical quantity the receiver can detect, such as voltage or light intensity.
questions.quizAnswer: Bits must be represented by detectable electrical, light or radio signals to cross the medium.
distractors: Bits must first be changed from binary to decimal because media cannot carry binary information.
Bits already travel as abstract numbers without any physical representation.
Only addressing data needs signals; application data does not need a physical representation.
questions.remember: Remember: Data is information; a signal is how that information physically travels.

questions.q: What are the properties of a good signal? [think of: easily detectable, resist noise, allowing multiplexing; efficient at using bandwidth]
questions.a:
Easy to detect
Resists noise
Allows multiplexing
Uses bandwidth efficiently
questions.practiceQ: What are the properties of a good signal? [think of: easily detectable, resist noise, allowing multiplexing; efficient at using bandwidth]
questions.explain: Reliable detection and resistance to noise reduce mistakes. Efficient bandwidth use increases useful data carried, while multiplexing allows multiple users to share the medium.
questions.quizAnswer: Easy detection, noise resistance, multiplexing support and efficient bandwidth use.
distractors: High amplitude alone, even if noise makes the signal impossible to distinguish.
Maximum bandwidth consumption, even when carrying very little useful data.
Good detection only when each user has a completely separate medium.
questions.remember: Remember: A receiver must distinguish the signal from noise. A useful signal must also use the available bandwidth efficiently.

questions.q: What are amplitude, frequency, phase, QAM modulations? Which one is better at what (bandwidth and noise resistance)?
questions.a:
Amplitude Modulation: Changes the strength/height of the signal.
Frequency modulation: changes how fast the wave cycles. 
Phase modulation: changes the position/phase of the wave. 
QAM – Quadrature Amplitude Modulation: combines changes in amplitude + phase to represent more bits.
QAM can send more data efficiently using available bandwidth, but more complex/high-order QAM is generally more sensitive to noise.
AM is vulnerable to amplitude noise. FM generally rejects amplitude noise better, often at the cost of greater bandwidth. Phase-based digital schemes can be power-efficient, but resistance depends on the particular scheme and order. High-order QAM improves spectral efficiency (bits per second per hertz) but requires a higher signal-to-noise ratio. No modulation is universally best.
questions.practiceQ: What are amplitude, frequency, phase, QAM modulations? Which one is better at what (bandwidth and noise resistance)?
questions.explain: Amplitude is wave height, frequency is cycle rate, and phase is position within a cycle. QAM changes amplitude and phase together. More QAM states encode more bits per symbol, but nearby states are easier for noise to confuse.
questions.quizAnswer: AM varies amplitude; FM varies frequency; PM varies phase; QAM combines amplitude and phase, trading higher efficiency for greater noise sensitivity at high orders.
distractors: AM varies frequency; FM varies amplitude; PM varies phase; QAM combines frequency and time slots.
AM varies amplitude; FM varies phase; PM varies frequency; higher-order QAM is always more noise-resistant.
AM varies amplitude; FM varies frequency; PM varies phase; QAM changes amplitude only and never phase.
questions.remember: Remember: AM changes strength, FM changes cycles per second, PM changes phase, and QAM changes amplitude and phase together.

questions.q: What is multiplexing? What are the two categories of multiplexing?
questions.a:
Multiplexing means allowing multiple signals/users to share the same communication medium. 
Two major categories:
FDM – Frequence Division Multiplexing: Different users get different frequency ranges
TDM – Time Division Multiplexing: Different users get different time slots.
Remember: 
FDM = Frequency
TDM = Time
questions.practiceQ: What is multiplexing? What are the two categories of multiplexing?
questions.explain: FDM separates users by frequency, like different radio stations. TDM separates users by time, like people taking turns speaking. Both share one medium without assigning each user a separate cable.
questions.quizAnswer: Multiplexing shares a medium: FDM uses separate frequency ranges and TDM uses separate time slots.
distractors: Multiplexing shares a medium: FDM uses time slots and TDM uses frequency ranges.
Multiplexing requires one separate physical medium for every user, so users never share.
FDM and TDM both assign separate frequency ranges; neither separates users in time.
questions.remember: Remember: Multiplexing shares one medium. FDM gives signals different frequency bands; TDM gives them different time slots.

questions.q: What are the primary functions of the data-link layer?
questions.a:
The Data Link Layer handles communication over a local network/link.
Major jobs: 
Creates frames
Uses MAC addresses
Detects transmission errors
Controls access to the local medium
questions.practiceQ: What are the primary functions of the data-link layer?
questions.explain: The data-link layer handles one local link. It packages data into frames, uses link-layer addresses, checks for transmission errors and manages access to the shared medium when needed.
questions.quizAnswer: Create frames, use MAC addresses, detect errors and control access to the local medium.
distractors: Choose IP routes between networks and replace every MAC address with an IP address.
Only convert bits into physical signals, without framing or error detection.
Manage application sessions and data compression, without local-link delivery.
questions.remember: Remember: Data Link handles a local frame: addressing it, controlling access to the link and detecting transmission errors.

questions.q: What are the components of a typical Ethernet? What are the functions of each component? (a cable, and hosts with NICs)
questions.a:
Cable -> carries the signal
Hosts with NICs -> devices connected to Ethernet.
A NIC (Network Interface Card) allows a device to connect to the network and has a MAC address.
questions.practiceQ: What are the components of a typical Ethernet? What are the functions of each component? (a cable, and hosts with NICs)
questions.explain: A cable supplies the signal path, while each NIC sends and receives on that path. The NIC gives the host a network interface; an Ethernet MAC address identifies an interface at the link layer.
questions.quizAnswer: The cable carries signals; hosts use NICs to connect, and NICs have MAC addresses.
distractors: The NIC carries signals between buildings without a medium; the cable stores the host’s MAC address.
Hosts need cables but no network interfaces, because a cable performs all NIC functions.
The cable selects routes between IP networks; the NIC’s only job is compressing application data.
questions.remember: Remember: A NIC connects a host to the network. The cable carries its signals; the host creates or uses the data.

questions.q: What is broadcast in the context of Ethernet? What are its advantages.
questions.a:
A broadcast sends a frame to every device on the local Ethernet network.
Advantage: Useful when the sender doesn’t know exactly which device needs to respond. Instead of it being sent only to one person, it’s sent to everyone.
questions.practiceQ: What is broadcast in the context of Ethernet? What are its advantages.
questions.explain: A broadcast reaches the whole local broadcast domain, which is helpful when a sender needs to discover an unknown participant. It does not mean sending to every computer on the Internet.
questions.quizAnswer: A frame sent throughout the local broadcast domain, useful when the correct responder is not yet known.
distractors: A frame addressed to exactly one already-known receiver, so no other local device receives it.
A frame that automatically reaches every device on the entire Internet.
A frame that reaches only the sending device and cannot discover other hosts.
questions.remember: Remember: A broadcast is addressed to everyone in the local broadcast domain. A shared medium being heard by everyone is not the same as every frame being a broadcast.

questions.q: What is Carrier Sensing Multiple Access with Collision Detection in Ethernet?
questions.a: CSMA/CD = Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. For shared, half-duplex Ethernet: sense the medium, transmit if idle, detect a collision, send a jam signal and stop, wait a random backoff interval, then retry. Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet does not use CSMA/CD.
questions.practiceQ: What is Carrier Sensing Multiple Access with Collision Detection in Ethernet?
questions.explain: Listening reduces collisions but cannot eliminate them: two devices may start together. Detection, stopping and randomized backoff let them retry at different times. This applies to shared half-duplex Ethernet, not switched full-duplex links.
questions.quizAnswer: Sense the medium, transmit if idle, detect a collision, stop and wait a randomized interval, then retry.
distractors: Transmit without sensing, continue through a collision, and never retry.
Sense the medium, then force every other device to keep waiting forever after one collision.
After a collision, all senders retry immediately at the same fixed instant.
questions.remember: Remember: On shared half-duplex Ethernet, listen before sending. After a collision, stop, signal it, wait randomly and retry.

questions.q: What is the size of the largest frame? 1518 Bytes (8 bytes preamble/SFD not counted; 14 bytes header, 1500 bytes payload, 4 bytes FCS)
questions.a: 1518 bytes is the maximum ordinary untagged Ethernet frame: 14-byte header + 1500-byte payload + 4-byte FCS. The 8 bytes of preamble/SFD are not counted. 1500 is the payload, not the whole frame. VLAN tags and jumbo frames change the size.
questions.practiceQ: What is the maximum ordinary untagged Ethernet frame size? How much is payload, header and FCS, and is preamble/SFD counted?
questions.explain: Do the addition: 14 bytes of header + 1500 bytes of payload + 4 bytes of FCS = 1518. The common confusion is calling the 1500-byte payload the whole frame. Preamble/SFD adds 8 bytes on the wire but is excluded from that frame count.
questions.quizAnswer: 1518 bytes: 14-byte header + 1500-byte payload + 4-byte FCS; preamble/SFD excluded.
distractors: 1500 bytes total: the header and FCS are already included in that payload value.
1526 bytes for the ordinary frame count because the 8-byte preamble/SFD must be counted.
1514 bytes total: 14-byte header + 1500-byte payload, with no FCS included.
questions.remember: Remember: The ordinary untagged maximum is 14 bytes of header + 1500 bytes of payload + 4 bytes of FCS = 1518 bytes.

questions.q: List the fields in the Ethernet header. What are the roles of each of these fields? Preamble +SFD; Destination Address; Source Address; Length/Type; Data from IP-Layer and Padding; FCS.
questions.a: On the wire: preamble (7 bytes) and SFD (1) synchronize/start; destination MAC (6) identifies the intended receiver; source MAC (6) identifies the sender; Length/Type (2) gives length or upper-layer protocol; data/padding carries the payload; FCS (4) detects errors. The ordinary header itself is destination + source + Length/Type, 14 bytes. Preamble/SFD, payload and FCS are not all header fields.
questions.practiceQ: List the Ethernet fields in transmission order and explain the role of each. Which fields form the ordinary header?
questions.explain: Synchronization comes first so the receiver can find the frame. Addresses identify who receives and who sent it, Type/Length describes the carried data, and FCS checks for corruption. Only destination, source and Type/Length form the ordinary 14-byte header.
questions.quizAnswer: Preamble/SFD synchronize/start; destination identifies receiver; source identifies sender; Type/Length describes data; payload/padding carry data; FCS detects errors.
distractors: Preamble/SFD synchronize/start; destination identifies sender; source identifies receiver; FCS detects errors.
Destination/source identify endpoints; Type/Length detects errors; FCS identifies the upper-layer protocol.
Preamble contains the payload; padding stores the source MAC; FCS synchronizes the start of transmission.
questions.remember: Remember: The frame identifies the destination and source, describes its contents, carries the data and ends with an error check.

questions.q: What is the structure of a MAC address? 48 bits (24 OUI of manufacturer; 24 host NIC unique #)
questions.a: A MAC address has 48 bits, usually written as six hexadecimal octets (for example 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E). In the traditional universally administered format, the first 24 bits are the OUI (manufacturer allocation), and the final 24 identify the interface within that allocation. Locally administered/randomized addresses do not necessarily identify a manufacturer.
questions.practiceQ: How is a traditional universally administered MAC address structured?
questions.explain: Each of the six hexadecimal octets contains 8 bits, so 6 × 8 = 48. In the traditional universal format, the first three octets identify the manufacturer allocation and the last three identify the interface within it.
questions.quizAnswer: 48 bits total: traditionally 24-bit OUI + 24-bit interface identifier.
distractors: 48 bits total: 16-bit OUI + 32-bit interface identifier.
32 bits total: 16-bit OUI + 16-bit interface identifier.
64 bits total: 24-bit OUI + 40-bit interface identifier.
questions.remember: Remember: A traditional MAC address is 48 bits: 24 bits for the manufacturer’s OUI and 24 bits to distinguish its interfaces.

questions.q: Know how to convert binary to decimal (vice versa); and binary to hex (vice versa)
questions.a:
For binary -> decimal:
128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1
00001010
8 + 2 = 10
For binary -> Hex, split into groups of 4 bits
1010 1111
1010 = A
1111 = F
Answer = AF
questions.practiceQ: Know how to convert binary to decimal (vice versa); and binary to hex (vice versa)
questions.explain: Binary place values double toward the left: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. Add only positions containing 1. Four bits have 16 combinations, so one hexadecimal digit exactly represents one four-bit group.
questions.quizAnswer: Binary place values are powers of 2; one hex digit represents 4 bits. 00001010₂ = 10₁₀ and 10101111₂ = AF₁₆.
distractors: Binary place values are powers of 10; one hex digit represents 8 bits. 00001010₂ = 1010₁₀.
Binary place values are powers of 2, but 00001010₂ = 12₁₀ and 10101111₂ = FA₁₆.
Binary digits are added without place values, so 00001010₂ = 2₁₀ and 1111₂ = 4₁₆.
questions.remember: Remember: For decimal, add the place values with a 1. For hexadecimal, split binary into four-bit groups.

questions.q: What is the difference between hubs and switches?
questions.a: A hub repeats incoming bits to other ports and shares a collision domain. A switch learns source MAC-to-port mappings and forwards known unicast frames to the matching port. A switch floods broadcast and unknown-unicast frames within the VLAN; it does not always send to just one port.
questions.practiceQ: What is the difference between hubs and switches?
questions.explain: A hub repeats signals without learning destinations. A switch learns which source MAC appears on which port, then uses that table for known unicast traffic. Broadcast and unknown destinations still require flooding within the VLAN.
questions.quizAnswer: A hub repeats incoming signals to other ports; a switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and forwards known unicast traffic selectively.
distractors: A switch repeats every signal without learning; a hub learns MAC addresses and selects destination ports.
Both hubs and switches learn IP routing tables and route between subnets as their defining function.
A hub and a switch behave identically: neither can learn which device is on a port.
questions.remember: Remember: A hub repeats signals to other ports. A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and uses them to forward frames.

questions.q: What is the spanning tree protocol? What is it used for?
questions.a:
STP prevents network loops when switches have multiple paths between them.
It can temporarily block redundant paths so frames don’t loop forever.
STP = prevents switching loops.
questions.practiceQ: What is the spanning tree protocol? What is it used for?
questions.explain: Redundant links can create loops in which Ethernet frames keep circulating. STP creates a loop-free forwarding tree by blocking selected redundant paths while retaining alternatives for failures.
questions.quizAnswer: STP prevents layer-2 loops by blocking selected redundant forwarding paths.
distractors: STP makes every redundant path forward each frame simultaneously to prevent loops.
STP assigns a new IP prefix to every frame so it can loop safely forever.
STP removes every backup cable permanently, rather than controlling forwarding.
questions.remember: Remember: Redundant switch links can make loops. STP blocks selected paths so the active topology has no loop.

questions.q: Different topologies
questions.a:
Star: devices connect to one central device
Bus: devices share one main cable
Ring: devices form a circle
Mesh: devices have multiple connections to each other
The most common Ethernet topology today is star
questions.practiceQ: Different topologies
questions.explain: Identify the shape: central connection means star; one shared cable means bus; a circle means ring; multiple interconnections mean mesh. A switched Ethernet LAN commonly has a physical star shape.
questions.quizAnswer: Star: central device; bus: shared cable; ring: circle; mesh: multiple interconnections. Star is common in Ethernet.
distractors: Star: shared cable; bus: central device; ring: circle; mesh: multiple interconnections.
Star: central device; bus: circle; ring: shared cable; mesh: no redundant connections.
Star: all devices directly connect to every other device; mesh: one central device only.
questions.remember: Remember: Star has a center, bus has a shared cable, ring forms a circle, and mesh has multiple interconnections.

questions.q: What is Routing? What are Routing Tables (hold all the routers information thus the network layout)
questions.a: Routing selects the next hop/path for packets between networks. Routing tables contain destination prefixes and forwarding information (such as next hop, interface and metrics). They need not contain the complete network topology.
questions.practiceQ: What is routing, and what information is stored in a routing table?
questions.explain: A router looks up the packet’s destination and chooses forwarding information for a matching prefix. The table needs routes and next hops; it does not have to store a complete map of every device.
questions.quizAnswer: Routing chooses packet paths/next hops between networks; routing tables contain destination routes and forwarding information.
distractors: Routing delivers only local MAC frames; routing tables contain only manufacturer OUIs.
Routing chooses cable signal amplitude; routing tables record only cable lengths.
Routing requires a complete list of every host and cable in the entire Internet in each router’s table.
questions.remember: Remember: A routing table tells a router where to send packets for destination networks. It is not a complete map of every router.

questions.q: What is the need for a computer address at the IP layer when computers also have a MAC address? layering independence (changing one without changing the other).
questions.a:
Because IP and MAC addresses serve different layers and purposes.
MAC address: local data link communication
IP address: communication/routing across networks.
Layering independence: one can change without requiring the other to change.
questions.practiceQ: Why is an IP address needed when a computer already has a MAC address?
questions.explain: IP identifies where to route across networks, while MAC addressing delivers a frame on the current local link. As a packet crosses routers, link-layer addressing can change while the IP destination remains the remote host.
questions.quizAnswer: IP supports addressing/routing across networks; MAC supports local-link delivery, keeping the layers independent.
distractors: IP and MAC are redundant names for the same address and can always replace one another.
MAC routes across networks; IP identifies only the next local Ethernet receiver.
An IP address is needed only to record the manufacturer of the NIC.
questions.remember: Remember: MAC is for local-link delivery; IP is for routing across networks. These separate jobs allow the addresses to change independently.

questions.q: The 2 parts of an IP address?
questions.a:
An ip address contains:
Network portion + Host portion
Network = which network?
Host = which device inside that network?
questions.practiceQ: The 2 parts of an IP address?
questions.explain: The prefix length determines which bits belong to the network. The remaining bits identify a host/interface within that subnet, so the split is not always at an octet boundary.
questions.quizAnswer: Network portion identifies the subnet; host portion identifies a host/interface within it.
distractors: Host portion identifies the subnet; network portion identifies the device within it.
The two parts are manufacturer OUI and a NIC-specific identifier.
The network and host portions are always exactly 16 bits each.
questions.remember: Remember: An IP prefix identifies the network. The remaining bits identify an interface within that network.

questions.q: Classless Inter Domain Routing (CIDR) notation and calculations: ex: 73.5.0.0/17 ;
questions.a:
/17 means 17 bits = network portion
IPv4 has 32 total bits, so:
32-17 = 15 host bits.
 Number of total addresses: 2^15 = 32,768 addresses
For traditional usable-host calculation:
32,768 – 2 = 32,766 usable hosts
The two traditionally reserved addresses are the network address and broadcast address.
questions.practiceQ: Classless Inter Domain Routing (CIDR) notation and calculations: ex: 73.5.0.0/17 ;
questions.explain: First find the host-bit count: IPv4 has 32 bits, so 32 − 17 = 15. Each host bit has two choices, giving 2¹⁵ = 32,768 total addresses. For this ordinary subnet, reserve one network address and one broadcast address: 32,768 − 2 = 32,766 usable host addresses.
questions.quizAnswer: /17 means 17 network bits and 15 host bits: 32,768 total addresses and traditionally 32,766 usable hosts.
distractors: /17 means 17 host bits and 15 network bits: 131,072 total addresses.
/17 means 17 network bits and 15 host bits: 32,766 total addresses and 32,768 usable hosts.
/17 means 17 network bytes and 15 host bytes: 32 total addresses.
questions.remember: Remember: Bits are positions; addresses are combinations. Subtract to count bits, raise 2 to that count for all addresses, then subtract 2 only when asked for usable hosts.

questions.q: How many objects can be uniquely labeled with 10-bit address labels? Hint (210 ) . You wish to assign unique labels to 200 objects using binary numbers. What is the minimum number of bits needed? Hint – start from somewhere 27 =128 (too few); 210 1024 (too many); 28 (just right; should be little bit above the target)
questions.a:
Rule:
With n bits, you can create 2^n unique combinations.
So with 10 bits:
2^10 = 1024
Therefore, 10-bit labels can uniquely label 1,024 objects
For 200 objects, find the smallest power of 2 that reaches at least 200:
2^7 = 128
2^8 = 256
Answer = 8 bits.
questions.practiceQ: How many objects can 10-bit labels uniquely identify? What is the minimum number of bits needed to label 200 objects?
questions.explain: Each additional bit doubles the number of possible labels. Ten bits give 1024 labels. For 200 objects, seven bits give only 128, while eight give 256, so eight is the minimum.
questions.quizAnswer: 10 bits label 1024 objects; 200 objects need at least 8 bits because 2^7 < 200 ≤ 2^8.
distractors: 10 bits label 1000 objects; 200 objects need 7 bits because 2^7 exceeds 200.
10 bits label 1024 objects; 200 objects need 200 bits, one bit per object.
10 bits label 20 objects; 200 objects need 100 bits because each bit labels two objects.
questions.remember: Remember: Each extra bit doubles the choices. Ten bits give 1024 labels; eight bits give 256, enough for 200 objects.

questions.q: What are the disadvantages of using address classes (A, B, C…)? How does CIDR overcome these disadvantages?
questions.a:
Old classful addressing used fixed sizes like Class A, B, and C.
Problem: wasted IP addresses because organizations were forced into fixed network sizes.
CIDR allows flexible prefix lengths like: /17, /20 /24, etc.
That lets networks receive an address block closer to the size they actually need.
Classes = rigid
CIDR = flexible
questions.practiceQ: What are the disadvantages of using address classes (A, B, C…)? How does CIDR overcome these disadvantages?
questions.explain: Fixed address classes force organizations into large predefined block sizes. CIDR changes the prefix length so allocations can fit more closely, reducing wasted addresses and supporting route aggregation.
questions.quizAnswer: Fixed class sizes waste addresses; CIDR uses flexible prefix lengths to fit allocations more closely.
distractors: CIDR wastes addresses by requiring every organization to use a fixed Class A block.
Address classes are flexible; CIDR replaces them with only three fixed block sizes.
CIDR eliminates the network/host split and therefore cannot express subnet sizes.
questions.remember: Remember: Fixed address classes offered rigid sizes. CIDR lets the prefix length change so allocations fit better.

questions.q: What is the correct representation of an IPv6 address
questions.a: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of up to four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. Leading zeros within groups may be omitted; one run of zero groups may be replaced by ::, at most once in an address. 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 compresses to 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334. 2001:db8::1 is a separate valid example, not a shortening of that address.
questions.practiceQ: What is the correct representation of an IPv6 address
questions.explain: Eight groups × 16 bits = 128 bits. Leading zeros can disappear inside a group, and :: fills in enough all-zero groups to bring the total back to eight. Using :: twice would make that reconstruction ambiguous.
questions.quizAnswer: 128 bits in eight hexadecimal groups separated by colons; omit leading zeros and use :: once for a run of zero groups.
distractors: 32 bits in four decimal groups separated by dots; :: can appear anywhere repeatedly.
128 bits in eight decimal groups separated by dots; each group must contain exactly one digit.
128 bits in hexadecimal, but :: can occur multiple times with no ambiguity.
questions.remember: Remember: IPv6 has eight 16-bit groups. Remove leading zeros within groups; use :: at most once for consecutive zero groups.

questions.q: ICMP utilities (ping, traceroute, pingpath)
questions.a: ICMP = Internet Control Message Protocol; it carries diagnostics and error/status messages. Ping uses echo request/reply to test reachability. Traceroute discovers hops using increasing TTL/hop limit and returned ICMP messages; probes vary by implementation. Windows pathping combines route tracing with loss/latency measurement. A blocked ping does not always mean the host is down.
questions.practiceQ: ICMP utilities (ping, traceroute, pingpath)
questions.explain: Ping asks whether an echo reply comes back. Traceroute reveals successive hops by making probes expire farther along the path. Pathping adds measurements over time. Missing replies can result from filtering, not just a failed host.
questions.quizAnswer: Ping tests reachability; traceroute shows hops; pathping adds loss/latency measurements; ICMP carries diagnostic/error messages.
distractors: Ping lists every hop; traceroute only measures cable bandwidth; pathping assigns IP addresses.
Ping changes the route; traceroute assigns MAC addresses; ICMP defines Ethernet cabling.
Ping tests reachability; traceroute shows hops; pathping is a physical cable, not a utility.
questions.remember: Remember: Ping checks for an echo reply, traceroute explores hops, and pathping adds loss and timing measurements over time.

questions.q: What are regional registries? What is the need for regional registries?
questions.a:
Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) manage and distribution IP addresses within different regions of the world. 
They’re needed so IP address allocation is organized and unique, instead of different organizations accidentally assigning overlapping public address space.
questions.practiceQ: What are regional registries? What is the need for regional registries?
questions.explain: A public IP address is an Internet-facing address that must be uniquely assigned for routing to work reliably. Allocation means assigning a block of addresses to an organization. RIRs coordinate these assignments within regions as part of the global registry system.
questions.quizAnswer: RIRs coordinate Internet-number allocation in geographic regions to keep public allocations organized and unique.
distractors: RIRs give every organization the same public address block to simplify routing.
RIRs assign the manufacturer half of every MAC address rather than IP resources.
RIRs are routers inside each building that broadcast all IP addresses to local hosts.
questions.remember: Remember: Imagine two unrelated towns receiving the same complete mailing addresses: deliveries become ambiguous. Registries coordinate assignments to avoid that conflict.

questions.q: What are the goals of network design and implementation?
questions.a: meet current and foreseeable end-user needs, using the most appropriate technology and addressing any organizational constraints in a manner that minimizes costs over a specified time period. Cost include initial setup + maintenance. If network too slow or unreliable there is cost of user downtime (users unable to perform their jobs).
questions.practiceQ: What are the goals of network design and implementation?
questions.explain: The cheapest purchase is not always the cheapest network. A design must account for future needs, maintenance and the cost of downtime as well as initial equipment and installation.
questions.quizAnswer: Meet present and foreseeable needs within constraints while minimizing costs over time, including setup, maintenance and downtime.
distractors: Minimize purchase price alone, even if users repeatedly cannot work.
Maximize speed at any cost without considering user needs or constraints.
Meet only today’s needs and exclude maintenance and future demand from planning.
questions.remember: Remember: A good design meets user needs now and later while considering equipment, maintenance and downtime costs.

questions.q: What are some of the important pieces of information you should gather during the requirements-analysis phase of network design?
questions.a: Identifying the different categories of users and applications + office locations so that network can support high bandwidth at required locations.
questions.practiceQ: What are some of the important pieces of information you should gather during the requirements-analysis phase of network design?
questions.explain: You must know who uses the network, which applications they run and where they work before estimating link capacity and placing equipment. Requirements drive the design decisions.
questions.quizAnswer: User categories, applications, office locations, capacity needs and constraints.
distractors: Only cable colors and equipment brand names, before considering users.
Only the number of routers, regardless of applications or user locations.
Only the initial purchase budget, excluding all performance requirements.
questions.remember: Remember: Before choosing equipment, find out who uses the network, which applications they use, where they work and how much traffic they generate.

questions.q: What is a logical network design?
questions.a: indicates the layout of the network, the subnets in the network, IP addressing and naming schemes used in the network and management strategies used in the network.  In Drawing.
questions.practiceQ: What is a logical network design?
questions.explain: Logical design describes how the network is organized: subnets, addressing, names and management. Physical design then chooses the actual media and devices that implement that plan.
questions.quizAnswer: A plan of network organization, subnets, addressing/naming and management strategies.
distractors: A list only of exact cable materials and switch model numbers.
An inventory only of broken devices awaiting repair.
A drawing only of electrical signal amplitudes on each cable.
questions.remember: Remember: Logical design is the plan for how the network is organized, not a shopping list of hardware.

questions.q: What are some important pieces of information you should show in a drawing of the logical network design?
questions.a: total number of general-purpose desktops, servers, shared devices such as printers, and any devices with special network needs for every area of the network
questions.practiceQ: What are some important pieces of information you should show in a drawing of the logical network design?
questions.explain: Device counts and special requirements help you size each area correctly. Desktops, servers and shared devices create different traffic demands and may need different connectivity.
questions.quizAnswer: Counts of desktops, servers, shared devices and devices with special network needs for each area.
distractors: Only desktops, since servers and printers do not affect network capacity.
Only the total number of buildings, with no devices shown in any area.
Only the brand of each cable, with no device counts or special requirements.
questions.remember: Remember: A logical drawing shows connections, subnets, addresses, device roles and services so the organization is clear.

questions.q: What is a physical network design?
questions.a: indicates the technologies (for example, copper/fiber media for cabling, switches, routers, data link layer technologies such as Ethernet) that will be used to implement the logical design.
questions.practiceQ: What is a physical network design?
questions.explain: Physical design turns a logical plan into installable choices: cabling, switches, routers and link technologies. It answers what equipment and media will make the logical connections real.
questions.quizAnswer: The media, equipment and technologies selected to implement the logical design.
distractors: Only the IP-addressing and naming plan, without specifying equipment or media.
Only the policy for choosing names, excluding switches and routers.
Only the user/application requirements, with no implementation choices.
questions.remember: Remember: Physical design turns the logical plan into real devices, cables, links and installation choices.

questions.q: What is a building network? Connects devices in a single building with Ethernet technology.
questions.a: A building network connects devices within one building, commonly through Ethernet switches and cabling plus wireless access points.
questions.practiceQ: What is a building network?
questions.explain: The boundary here is one building. Devices usually connect through Ethernet switches and cabling, with wireless access points also providing local connectivity.
questions.quizAnswer: A network connecting devices within a single building, commonly using Ethernet.
distractors: A network defined by connecting multiple nearby buildings rather than one building.
A network defined by geographically scattered offices connected through WAN services.
A network that requires every device to be in the same room, not merely the same building.
questions.remember: Remember: A building network connects devices within one building, commonly with Ethernet switches and wireless access points.

questions.q: Components of a structured cabling + horizontal/vertical cabling.
questions.a:
Structured cabling is an organized cabling system for a building.
Horizontal cabling: runs from telecommunications/network rooms to individual work areas/devices on a floor.
Vertical cabling/backbone connects different floors or telecommunications rooms.
Common structured-cabling components include the entrance facility, equipment room, backbone cabling, telecommunications rooms, horizontal cabling and work areas; patch panels organize terminations.
questions.practiceQ: Components of a structured cabling + horizontal/vertical cabling.
questions.explain: Horizontal cabling serves work areas on a floor; vertical/backbone cabling joins rooms or floors. Structured cabling organizes these paths and termination points so installation and maintenance are predictable.
questions.quizAnswer: Structured cabling organizes building wiring; horizontal serves work areas on a floor, vertical/backbone joins floors or rooms.
distractors: Horizontal cabling joins different floors; vertical cabling connects desks on one floor.
Horizontal and vertical both describe IP address portions, not cable paths.
Structured cabling means every device must connect directly to every other device.
questions.remember: Remember: Horizontal cabling reaches work areas. Vertical or backbone cabling joins telecommunications spaces.

questions.q: Data Center Topology
questions.a:
A data center topology is the layout showing how servers and networking equipment are interconnected inside a data center. 
The key idea is supporting fast, reliable communication between large numbers, of servers. 
Examples include traditional tiered designs and spine-leaf: servers connect to leaf switches, and each leaf connects to each spine, giving predictable paths and redundant capacity.
questions.practiceQ: Data Center Topology
questions.explain: Many servers exchange traffic with one another, so the topology must support capacity and resilience. In a spine-leaf example, every leaf connects to every spine, giving multiple predictable paths.
questions.quizAnswer: The arrangement of server/network connections to support fast, reliable communication among many servers.
distractors: Only the assignment of individual server passwords, not their interconnections.
Only the public IP allocation for a whole geographic region.
The requirement that all server traffic must use one unprotected shared cable.
questions.remember: Remember: In leaf-spine, every leaf connects to every spine. Link capacity still determines how much traffic it can carry.

questions.q: What is a campus network? Multiple buildings with 3 layers (core, distribution, access)
questions.a: A campus network connects multiple nearby buildings. A common hierarchical design has Core → Distribution → Access layers.
questions.practiceQ: What is a campus network, and what are its three hierarchical layers?
questions.explain: A campus joins nearby buildings. The access layer connects devices, distribution aggregates and applies policy, and the core provides fast transport between distribution areas.
questions.quizAnswer: A campus connects multiple nearby buildings; a common hierarchy is Core → Distribution → Access.
distractors: A campus connects a single workstation only; its hierarchy is Access → Core → Distribution.
A campus is always geographically scattered across distant cities with no nearby buildings.
A campus has the hierarchy Application → Presentation → Session instead of network-design tiers.
questions.remember: Remember: A campus joins nearby buildings. Its common three layers are Access, Distribution and Core.

questions.q: What is the role of the core layer? Connected to all parts (all traffic passes through), fast and reliable data transport, called backbone.
questions.a:
The core is the network’s backbone.
It provides
Fast transportation
Reliable transportation
Connections between different parts of the network
A lot of network traffic passes through it.
Core = fast backbone.
questions.practiceQ: What is the role of the core layer?
questions.explain: In Chapter 12's campus design, distribution regions need fast, reliable connections to one another. The core supplies that backbone capacity.
questions.quizAnswer: Fast, reliable backbone transport linking major parts of the network.
distractors: Providing individual users with their first network connection as its primary role.
Formatting and encrypting application data as an OSI layer.
Replacing all distribution-layer policies with individual desktop ports.
questions.remember: Remember: Picture the main highways between neighborhoods, not the port where one student plugs in.

questions.q: What are the roles of the distribution layer? Administrative layer, organizes subnets, responsible for firewalls, and authentication (thus internet connectivity to the outside world).
questions.a: The distribution layer aggregates access networks, routes between subnets and applies policies such as filtering and access control. The guide associates it with firewalls, authentication and external connectivity; exact service placement depends on the design.
questions.practiceQ: What are the roles of the distribution layer?
questions.explain: Access networks need to be brought together and connected toward the backbone. This is a common location for routing between subnets and applying policy. The placement of firewalls and authentication services depends on the particular design.
questions.quizAnswer: Aggregate access networks, organize/route between subnets and apply administrative/security policies.
distractors: Primarily provide a single end-user port at every desk, with no aggregation role.
Only send raw electrical/light signals, with no policy or subnet role.
Only act as the fastest backbone, never performing administrative policy functions.
questions.remember: Remember: Gather neighborhood traffic and decide how it can move toward other areas.

questions.q: What service is offered by the access layer? Providing network ports to end users, includes hubs/switches, organizing the devices in a building into Ethernets.
questions.a: The access layer connects end-user devices through network ports and wireless access points, normally using switches; it can assign devices to VLANs/Ethernet segments.
questions.practiceQ: What service is offered by the access layer?
questions.explain: Computers, printers and access points need their first connection to the campus network. Access switches supply that edge connectivity.
questions.quizAnswer: Connect end-user devices through network ports and access equipment.
distractors: Provide only the high-speed backbone between distribution regions.
Allocate public address blocks to organizations throughout a region.
Choose the organization’s standards approval procedure.
questions.remember: Remember: Start at the user's device and follow its first network cable.

questions.q: What is an enterprise network? organization’s geographically scattered network (ISPs provide WAN connectivity). An enterprise network connects and organization’s networks across geographically separated locations.
questions.a: An enterprise network connects an organization’s networks across geographically separated locations. ISPs can provide the WAN connectivity connection those locations.
questions.practiceQ: What is an enterprise network? How are its distant locations connected?
questions.explain: Enterprise networks can span distant locations. WAN services supplied by providers connect those sites into the organization’s broader network.
questions.quizAnswer: An organization’s networks across geographically separated locations, often joined using provider WAN connectivity.
distractors: Only one floor’s horizontal cabling, with no connections beyond that floor.
Only nearby buildings on a single campus; distant sites are excluded by definition.
A shared Ethernet frame format that does not describe organizational networks.
questions.remember: Remember: An enterprise may have far-apart sites. WAN services connect those locations.

questions.q: What are the important activities in network maintenance? inspection, testing, and servicing of devices and software, monitoring, updating both HW and SW.
questions.a: Network maintenance includes inspection, testing, servicing, monitoring, configuration/backup management, and updating hardware and software.
questions.practiceQ: What are the important activities in network maintenance?
questions.explain: Maintenance combines prevention and response: inspect and test, monitor for changes, service equipment, protect configurations and keep hardware/software current. Waiting for a failure is only one part of the job.
questions.quizAnswer: Inspection, testing, servicing, monitoring and hardware/software updates.
distractors: Initial installation only; nothing is needed once users connect.
Waiting for complete failure without monitoring or routine inspection.
Changing cable categories daily without checking equipment or software.
questions.remember: Remember: Maintenance means looking after the network before and after problems: inspect, test, monitor, service and update.

questions.q: What is a Simple Network Management Protocol?
questions.a: With SNMP, the management application on the network management station can poll all the managed elements (configurations, fan speed, temps etc), say, once per hour and observe the status of all the information items. If discrepancy  alert the admin via email, SMS etc.
questions.practiceQ: What is a Simple Network Management Protocol?
questions.explain: SNMP separates the manager from agents on devices. The manager can poll values such as temperatures or interface counters, while device notifications can flag events that need attention.
questions.quizAnswer: Simple Network Management Protocol lets a management system query device information and monitor status.
distractors: Simple Network Management Protocol chooses loop-free Ethernet paths by blocking links.
Simple Network Management Protocol assigns every host its MAC manufacturer identifier.
Simple Network Management Protocol replaces all raw bits with optical signals.
questions.remember: Remember: SNMP lets a manager ask agents on devices for management information and, when authorized, change supported settings.

questions.q: What is the Management Information Base (MIB)? an information store that contains information which is essential for fault management
questions.a: MIB = Management Information Base. A structured collection of managed objects, identified by object identifiers (OIDs), that management software can query through SNMP; supports monitoring and fault management.
questions.practiceQ: What is the Management Information Base (MIB)?
questions.explain: Managed objects have defined names, types and meanings so management software can interpret device values consistently. Agents expose the actual values described by these definitions.
questions.quizAnswer: A structured Management Information Base containing information used for monitoring and fault management.
distractors: A table containing only routes to remote IP networks, with no device-management information.
The payload part of an Ethernet frame, excluding all management information.
A physical store of spare cables used instead of monitoring data.
questions.remember: Remember: The MIB explains the dashboard gauges; the agent supplies their readings.

questions.q: What are standards? Consensus documents having rules, guidelines  interoperability.
questions.a: Standards are consensus specifications/rules/guidelines that support interoperability and consistent behavior.
questions.practiceQ: What are standards?
questions.explain: Shared specifications reduce the chance that each vendor implements an incompatible interpretation. Interoperability is the central reason standards matter in networking.
questions.quizAnswer: Consensus specifications and guidelines supporting interoperability.
distractors: Private rules deliberately preventing different vendors from communicating.
Temporary device readings such as temperature, rather than agreed specifications.
Unique labels assigned to hosts, rather than rules for implementations.
questions.remember: Remember: A standard is a shared specification that helps independently made products work together.

questions.q: What is the typical procedure by which a standard is developed? Lead organization (ex: Institute Electrical Electronics Engineers; IEEE  for LAN/WLAN; Internet Engineering Task Force; IETF)  for TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP) create Working Groups which specify requirements  companies give technical solutions  members of lead org vote on the best solution.
questions.a: A standards organization establishes a working group, defines requirements, develops and reviews technical proposals, reaches agreement and publishes a specification. The exact process varies: IEEE uses working groups and ballots; IETF emphasizes rough consensus and technical review rather than simply a majority vote for a best vendor solution.
questions.practiceQ: What is the typical procedure by which a networking standard is developed?
questions.explain: Standards require shared technical requirements, proposals, review and agreement before publication. Procedures differ by organization; IEEE ballots and IETF rough consensus are not identical processes.
questions.quizAnswer: Define requirements in a working group, develop/review proposals, reach agreement and publish; exact procedures vary by organization.
distractors: Publish a final standard first, then decide the requirements without technical review.
Let each vendor choose incompatible rules without a shared review process.
Allow only end users to vote on cable colors, with no technical requirements or proposals.
questions.remember: Remember: Standards start with a need, then requirements, proposals, review and agreement. IEEE and IETF do not use identical approval procedures.

vocabExplanations.Layering: A browser can keep requesting pages after you switch from Ethernet to Wi-Fi because the lower-layer delivery details can change without changing the web request format.
vocabExplanations.Protocol: Two devices must agree on message format and meaning. If one sends a request the other cannot interpret, a working cable alone cannot make them communicate.
vocabExplanations.TCP/IP: TCP handles an ordered conversation between programs; IP handles packet addressing across networks. The suite also includes other protocols, so these two names label a larger family.
vocabExplanations.Application layer: HTTP gives a browser and web server rules for requests and replies. Those services are close to the program's purpose, while lower layers handle delivery.
vocabExplanations.Transport layer: One computer may run a browser and a mail app together. Transport ports distinguish the application endpoints so incoming data reaches the appropriate conversation.
vocabExplanations.Network layer: A destination can be several networks away. Routers read the destination IP address and choose a next hop, which explains why addressing and routing belong together here.
vocabExplanations.Data Link layer: An IP packet needs a local wrapper to cross a particular link. Ethernet adds MAC addresses and an error check to form that wrapper, called a frame.
vocabExplanations.Physical layer: A bit is an idea, not something a receiver can directly sense. The sender represents bits using voltage, light or radio so the receiver can measure them.
vocabExplanations.OSI: A common seven-job reference helps people compare network designs and locate faults even when vendors build different products.
vocabExplanations.Presentation layer: A receiver needs to interpret a sender's representation of data. The OSI Presentation role covers format translation and concepts such as compression and encryption.
vocabExplanations.Session layer: A continuing exchange needs a way to begin, coordinate and end the conversation. OSI names this conversation-management responsibility separately.
vocabExplanations.Encapsulation: Each delivery layer adds its own control information: transport ports, then IP addresses, then local-link information. The previous unit becomes the next wrapper's contents.
vocabExplanations.Decapsulation: The receiver processes the outer delivery information before passing the remaining contents upward. This lets the application receive its message without treating Ethernet labels as application data.
vocabExplanations.IEEE: IEEE's 802 standards families include wired Ethernet and wireless LAN rules. Shared specifications let interfaces made by different vendors use the same link technology.
vocabExplanations.IETF: Internet protocols must work across networks made by many organizations. IETF participants develop shared technical specifications through an open standards process.
vocabExplanations.LAN: A classroom's computers and printer can communicate through local switches without being a nationwide network. The limited geographic scope makes this a LAN.
vocabExplanations.WLAN: Wi-Fi devices exchange local traffic through radio rather than requiring a cable to each device. The network is still local in scope.
vocabExplanations.TCP: TCP tracks sequence numbers and acknowledgments, retransmitting when necessary and presenting bytes in order to the receiving application.
vocabExplanations.IP: IP packets carry source and destination addresses so routers can forward them toward another network. IP itself does not guarantee arrival or order.
vocabExplanations.DNS: People use readable names, while network software needs records such as an IP address. DNS queries obtain those records from a distributed naming system.
vocabExplanations.HTTP: A browser sends a request for a resource, and a server responds with a status and content. HTTP defines the meaning and format of that exchange.
vocabExplanations.Interoperability: A computer and switch from different vendors can communicate when both implement compatible rules. Matching the shared specification matters more than matching the logo.
vocabExplanations.Physical medium: A signal needs somewhere to travel. Copper, optical fiber and radio space provide different paths with different distance and interference limits.
vocabExplanations.Copper cable: Copper conductors allow electrical signal changes to travel between interfaces. Noise and signal loss affect how well the receiver can distinguish the changes.
vocabExplanations.Fiber-optic cable: A transmitter launches light into fiber and a receiver detects it. Because information is carried optically, electromagnetic interference does not induce electrical noise in the glass.
vocabExplanations.Wireless: An antenna sends and receives electromagnetic signals through space. A cable is not needed between the radio endpoints, but interference and obstacles still affect reception.
vocabExplanations.UTP: Pairs of copper conductors are twisted to help reduce unwanted coupling and interference. Unshielded means there is no metallic cable shielding around those pairs.
vocabExplanations.EMI: A nearby electromagnetic source can disturb an electrical signal and make its intended values harder to detect. This is unwanted energy, not useful data.
vocabExplanations.Crosstalk: A signal in one nearby pair can couple into another pair. Twisting and proper cable construction help limit that unwanted interaction.
vocabExplanations.Bandwidth: In signal math, bandwidth is a frequency range measured in hertz. In everyday network discussion the word may refer to data capacity, so the units tell you which meaning applies.
vocabExplanations.Bit rate: Counting how many bits are transmitted each second gives a data rate. A symbol may represent more than one bit, so bit rate is not always symbol rate.
vocabExplanations.Gbps: The lower-case b means bits. Dividing a bit rate by eight gives a byte-rate equivalent before allowing for overhead and other limits.
vocabExplanations.Noise: Random unwanted changes can make one intended signal value look like another. A receiver needs enough separation between valid signal states to tell them apart.
vocabExplanations.Attenuation: Signals lose strength as they travel. If a signal becomes too weak relative to noise, the receiver may no longer distinguish the intended values.
vocabExplanations.Cat 5e: The category specifies cable performance, while Ethernet standards determine supported links. A properly installed Cat 5e channel commonly supports gigabit Ethernet to 100 m.
vocabExplanations.Cat 6: Cat 6 supports gigabit Ethernet to 100 m, but 10-gigabit operation has shorter distance limits that depend on installation conditions.
vocabExplanations.Cat 6a: The augmented category improves performance for 10GBASE-T over a full 100 m channel when properly installed.
vocabExplanations.Cat 8: Cat 8 uses shielding and supports short 25/40-gigabit copper channels up to 30 m. Calling it unshielded or assigning it the usual 100 m reach would miss its key limits.
vocabExplanations.Total internal reflection: At a suitable angle, light traveling in the higher-index core reflects at the lower-index cladding boundary instead of escaping. That helps guide it along the fiber.
vocabExplanations.Core: In fiber, the central optical region guides the light. This is a material part of a cable, unrelated to the campus design tier also called Core.
vocabExplanations.Cladding: Its lower refractive index creates the boundary that helps confine light to the core. It is an optical part, unlike the outer protective jacket.
vocabExplanations.Single-mode fiber: A small core supports one spatial propagation mode, avoiding the multiple-path spreading associated with multimode fiber. Suitable optics make long links possible.
vocabExplanations.Multimode fiber: Different modes can take different paths and arrival times, spreading a pulse. The larger core supports these modes, and the optics and fiber grade determine usable reach.
vocabExplanations.Amplitude: Amplitude describes how far a signal moves from its reference level. Raising a wave's height changes amplitude without necessarily changing its cycles per second.
vocabExplanations.Frequency: If a wave repeats more cycles each second, its frequency increases. Hertz means cycles per second, not bits per second.
vocabExplanations.Phase: Two waves can have the same height and frequency but be shifted relative to each other. That relative position within the cycle is phase.
vocabExplanations.Modulation: A carrier is varied in a controlled way so its states represent information. The receiver detects those changes to recover the encoded information.
vocabExplanations.AM: Information is represented by amplitude changes. Unwanted amplitude changes can therefore imitate part of the message and cause confusion.
vocabExplanations.FM: Information is represented by changes in cycle rate. Amplitude disturbances are less directly confused with the encoded quantity, though performance depends on the system.
vocabExplanations.PM: Information is represented by shifts in the carrier's phase relative to a reference. A phase shift differs from simply making the wave taller.
vocabExplanations.QAM: Combining amplitude and phase creates multiple distinguishable symbol states. More states can carry more bits per symbol, but closer states require cleaner reception.
vocabExplanations.Multiplexing: Several streams share a resource by separating their use, such as into frequency bands or time slots. They do not each need a dedicated physical cable.
vocabExplanations.FDM: Separate frequency bands let streams occupy the same medium simultaneously. A receiver selects the appropriate band, like tuning a radio station.
vocabExplanations.TDM: Streams use assigned time intervals on the same resource. Taking turns separates them even when the same frequency range is reused.
vocabExplanations.Ethernet: Ethernet defines wired link behavior including frames and MAC addressing. IP can be carried inside Ethernet, but Ethernet and IP solve different delivery jobs.
vocabExplanations.Frame: A local-link receiver needs addressing and error-check information around the carried data. That header/payload/trailer unit is the frame.
vocabExplanations.Packet: IP adds a network-layer header around the transport data. A link then carries this whole unit as its payload.
vocabExplanations.Payload: What counts as payload depends on which wrapper you are discussing. A full IP packet is Ethernet payload, including the IP header.
vocabExplanations.NIC: A host needs an interface that can transmit and receive using the link technology. The NIC provides that connection rather than choosing Internet routes for every remote network.
vocabExplanations.MAC: Media Access Control concerns local link access and addressing. An Ethernet MAC address identifies an interface for local frame delivery.
vocabExplanations.OUI: In a traditional universally assigned MAC address, the first three byte pairs identify an IEEE-assigned organization prefix. The remaining part is assigned within that block.
vocabExplanations.Broadcast: One local message may need to reach everyone in a broadcast domain, for example during discovery. Routers normally stop Ethernet broadcasts from spreading into other networks.
vocabExplanations.Unicast: The destination identifies one recipient rather than a group. A switch with a known destination mapping can choose that recipient's port.
vocabExplanations.CSMA/CD: On shared half-duplex Ethernet, simultaneous starts can collide even after listening. Detecting a collision and waiting different random times lets devices retry.
vocabExplanations.Collision: Two transmissions overlap on a shared half-duplex medium, preventing successful reception. Each sender must retry according to the access rules.
vocabExplanations.Backoff: If both senders retried after the same delay, they could collide again. Randomized waits reduce the chance of synchronized retries.
vocabExplanations.Full duplex: Separate sending and receiving paths allow both endpoints to transmit at once. This removes the shared-medium collision situation in switched Ethernet.
vocabExplanations.Half duplex: Both directions are supported, but the shared resource cannot carry both transmissions simultaneously without conflict.
vocabExplanations.Preamble: A known alternating pattern helps the receiver synchronize before the frame begins. It is not a destination address or application payload.
vocabExplanations.SFD: After synchronization, a distinct one-byte pattern marks the start boundary so the receiver knows where frame fields begin.
vocabExplanations.Destination MAC: A switch uses the destination field to decide where a frame should go on the local network. Across a router, a new link frame uses the next local destination.
vocabExplanations.Source MAC: Switches learn which MAC addresses are reachable through incoming ports by examining the source field.
vocabExplanations.EtherType: The receiver must know how to interpret the payload. EtherType says which protocol, such as IPv4 or IPv6, follows the Ethernet header.
vocabExplanations.Padding: A short payload needs extra bytes so the Ethernet frame reaches its minimum size. Padding does not turn into additional meaningful application data.
vocabExplanations.FCS: The sender computes a check value over the frame and includes it at the end. A receiver compares its own calculation to detect corruption.
vocabExplanations.CRC: CRC is the calculation that produces a check value. FCS is the field carrying that value in an Ethernet frame.
vocabExplanations.MTU: An Ethernet IP MTU of 1500 counts the carried network-layer packet. Adding the Ethernet header and FCS makes a larger frame.
