vocabExplanations.Bit: One binary position has two possible values, so each additional bit doubles the number of possible combinations.
vocabExplanations.Byte: Grouping eight binary digits creates 2⁸ = 256 possible patterns. Network sizes in bytes therefore differ by a factor of eight from sizes in bits.
vocabExplanations.Octet: The word explicitly means eight bits. Each dotted decimal IPv4 part represents one such eight-bit group.
vocabExplanations.Nibble: Four bits have 16 possible patterns, matching exactly the 16 hexadecimal digit values.
vocabExplanations.Binary: The position values double as you move left: 1, 2, 4, 8. Add only the values whose digit is 1.
vocabExplanations.Decimal: Each position is ten times the one on its right. For example, 42 means four tens and two ones.
vocabExplanations.Hexadecimal: Each position is sixteen times the one on its right. A through F provide single symbols for values 10 through 15.
vocabExplanations.Hub: A hub repeats a received signal without reading a learned destination table. Connected half-duplex devices share the same collision domain.
vocabExplanations.Switch: A switch learns from source MAC addresses and looks up destination MAC addresses when forwarding. Unknown unicast and broadcasts are flooded within their VLAN.
vocabExplanations.STP: Extra switch links provide alternatives but can also form forwarding loops. STP blocks selected paths so active forwarding remains loop-free.
vocabExplanations.Topology: A topology shows how devices and connections are arranged. Physical wiring and the logical flow of traffic may have different shapes.
vocabExplanations.Star topology: Each endpoint has its own link to a central device. That central connection pattern is the identifying feature.
vocabExplanations.Bus topology: Multiple devices share a common main path. The shared backbone, rather than a separate center-to-endpoint link for each device, identifies a bus.
vocabExplanations.Ring topology: Each part connects along a loop that returns to its starting point. The circular connection structure identifies the ring.
vocabExplanations.Mesh topology: Multiple interconnections create alternative paths. In a full mesh, every pair is directly connected; a partial mesh has fewer links.
vocabExplanations.VLAN: A switch can separate ports into logical broadcast domains. Frames in one VLAN do not simply become local broadcasts in every other VLAN.
vocabExplanations.Router: A router uses destination IP prefixes and forwarding information to move packets between networks. A basic Layer-2 switch instead forwards local frames by MAC address.
vocabExplanations.Routing: A forwarding decision chooses the next step toward a destination. Each router makes its own decision using its available routes.
vocabExplanations.Routing table: Entries associate destination prefixes with an outgoing interface or next hop. A router matches the packet's destination against these entries.
vocabExplanations.Next hop: A packet may need several routers to reach its final destination. The next hop is just the immediately following forwarding stop.
vocabExplanations.IPv4: Four groups of eight bits give 32 bits total. Decimal dots make the groups easier to read, but routers work with the bit values.
vocabExplanations.IPv6: Eight groups of sixteen bits give 128 bits. Hexadecimal provides a compact representation, and zero compression can shorten it further.
vocabExplanations.Network portion: The prefix identifies the subnet shared by its members. Two interfaces in that subnet can share those bits while differing in the remaining positions.
vocabExplanations.Host portion: The bits after the prefix can vary within the subnet. Their patterns create address choices, although ordinary IPv4 subnets reserve the all-zero and all-one patterns.
vocabExplanations.CIDR: A variable prefix length lets the address block size match needs more closely than the old fixed classes. The slash number counts network bits.
vocabExplanations.Prefix length: IPv4 contains 32 positions. Reserving 17 for the network leaves 15 for the host portion, so /17 is not a count of hosts.
vocabExplanations.Subnet mask: Mask ones select the network portion and mask zeros identify the host portion. A /24 mask has 24 ones followed by eight zeros.
vocabExplanations.Network address: Setting all host bits to zero gives the first address of an ordinary subnet. That value names the subnet rather than an individual host.
vocabExplanations.Broadcast address: Setting all host bits to one gives the final address of an ordinary IPv4 subnet. It is reserved for reaching the subnet rather than assigning it to one interface.
vocabExplanations.Classful addressing: Fixed class sizes can force an organization to accept far more addresses than needed. CIDR varies the prefix instead of forcing those fixed sizes.
vocabExplanations.Hextet: Four hexadecimal digits each represent four bits, so one full IPv6 group represents sixteen bits. Omitted leading zeros do not change its width.
vocabExplanations.Zero compression: The receiver counts the written groups and fills the remaining positions with zeros. Two separate double colons would not say how to divide the missing groups.
vocabExplanations.ICMP: IP delivery needs a way to report conditions such as an unreachable destination or an expired hop limit. ICMP carries that control information.
vocabExplanations.Ping: Echo requests ask an endpoint to send an echo reply. The elapsed time measures a round trip, but filtering can block replies even when a device exists.
vocabExplanations.Traceroute: Probes with gradually increasing TTL or hop limits expire at progressively later routers. Replies can reveal those forwarding stops.
vocabExplanations.Pathping: It first discovers a route and then gathers probe statistics over time. That gives more loss and delay information than one simple reachability check.
vocabExplanations.TTL: Each router reduces the IPv4 TTL; a packet is discarded when it expires. This prevents a routing loop from keeping the packet alive indefinitely.
vocabExplanations.Latency: Latency measures waiting time for data to travel. A link can have a high data rate and still have a long delay because the destination is far away.
vocabExplanations.Packet loss: Some transmitted packets never arrive, for example because of congestion or corruption. Loss is a missing delivery, unlike latency's delayed delivery.
vocabExplanations.RIR: Public IP address blocks must be coordinated so unrelated networks are not assigned overlapping space. Regional registries manage that allocation and registration within their regions.
vocabExplanations.ARIN: ARIN is one of the regional organizations coordinating Internet number resources. Its service region includes the United States, Canada and parts of the Caribbean.
vocabExplanations.RIPE NCC: RIPE NCC coordinates Internet number resources for its service region, including Europe, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia.
vocabExplanations.APNIC: APNIC performs the regional Internet-number registry role for the Asia-Pacific service region.
vocabExplanations.LACNIC: LACNIC coordinates Internet number resources for Latin America and parts of the Caribbean.
vocabExplanations.AFRINIC: AFRINIC serves the African region in coordinating Internet number resources. It is one member of the regional registry system.
vocabExplanations.Requirements analysis: A design depends on who uses the network, which applications matter and what constraints exist. Buying equipment first can solve the wrong problem.
vocabExplanations.Logical design: Subnets, address plans and intended connectivity describe how the network should be organized without yet fixing every cable and device choice.
vocabExplanations.Physical design: The abstract connectivity plan must become actual equipment, media and placement. These installable choices form the physical design.
vocabExplanations.Building network: The scope is one building, even if it has many rooms, floors, switches or Wi-Fi access points.
vocabExplanations.Structured cabling: Predictable cabling paths, rooms and termination points make moves and repairs easier than a collection of improvised individual runs.
vocabExplanations.Horizontal cabling: Work-area outlets connect back to a local telecommunications room. Its role is serving those work areas, even if a cable bends or changes height.
vocabExplanations.Vertical cabling: Backbone cabling joins distribution spaces, floors or buildings. It links the local cabling areas rather than serving each desk directly.
vocabExplanations.Patch panel: Permanent cable runs terminate at labeled ports, allowing patch cords to connect them to equipment neatly. The panel itself does not route or switch packets.
vocabExplanations.Telecommunications room: Cable terminations and local network equipment need an organized service location. Horizontal runs typically connect work areas back to this space.
vocabExplanations.Data center: Servers, storage, networking, power and cooling are grouped to support applications reliably. It is a facility, not a numbered protocol layer.
vocabExplanations.Data center topology: Server-to-server traffic needs capacity and alternate paths. The way leaf and spine switches interconnect affects those paths and resilience.
vocabExplanations.Spine-leaf: Each leaf connects to every spine, allowing traffic between leaves through available spines. This creates predictable paths and alternatives if a path fails.
vocabExplanations.Campus network: Nearby buildings are joined into one organized local environment, such as a university campus. The scope differs from one building or distant branch offices.
vocabExplanations.Core layer: In Chapter 12's campus design, distribution regions need fast, reliable connections to one another. The core supplies that backbone capacity.
vocabExplanations.Distribution layer: Access networks need to be brought together and connected toward the backbone. This is a common location for routing between subnets and applying policy.
vocabExplanations.Access layer: Computers, printers and access points need their first connection to the campus network. Access switches supply that edge connectivity.
vocabExplanations.Backbone: Many smaller network areas depend on a main interconnection path. Carrying their combined traffic makes its capacity and reliability especially important.
vocabExplanations.Enterprise network: An organization may join local networks across buildings and distant sites. Enterprise describes the organization's combined network, not one required topology.
vocabExplanations.WAN: Distant local networks need broad-area connectivity, often through a provider. The geographic reach distinguishes WAN from LAN.
vocabExplanations.ISP: The provider connects customers to other networks and the Internet. It may also sell services linking an organization's distant sites.
vocabExplanations.Firewall: Traffic is checked against configured rules and allowed or denied. Rules can distinguish permitted communication from unwanted access.
vocabExplanations.Authentication: Before trusting an identity, a system checks evidence such as a password or credential. Permission to perform a particular action is a separate authorization decision.
vocabExplanations.Network maintenance: Monitoring, testing, backups and updates help detect faults, recover from failures and keep the installed system useful.
vocabExplanations.Downtime: When a service is unavailable, people may be unable to work even though no new equipment is being purchased. That lost work is part of network cost.
vocabExplanations.SNMP: Management software exchanges requests and notifications with agents on devices. This lets an administrator check values remotely instead of visiting every device.
vocabExplanations.MIB: Managed objects have defined names, types and meanings so management software can interpret device values consistently. Agents expose the actual values described by these definitions.
vocabExplanations.OID: A hierarchical numeric identifier names a managed object unambiguously. A manager can request a particular object rather than asking for an unnamed number.
vocabExplanations.Polling: A manager periodically asks for values so it can notice changes over time. This differs from a device sending an event notification on its own.
vocabExplanations.SNMP agent: Software on the managed device receives requests, accesses supported management values and returns results. An agent is not the administrator using the dashboard.
vocabExplanations.SNMP trap: An agent can send an event report without waiting for the manager to ask. A trap differs from a response to a periodic poll.
vocabExplanations.Standard: Independent builders need an agreed specification for compatible behavior. Following the same rules helps their products exchange meaningful messages.
vocabExplanations.Working group: People with technical expertise discuss proposals, resolve problems and develop specifications. In the IETF, decisions use rough consensus rather than simply counting votes.

understanding.q: A network changes the medium carrying its signals without redesigning all the application software. Which benefit of layering does this illustrate?
understanding.answer: One layer can change while other layers keep their roles.
options: One layer can change while other layers keep their roles.
Changing one layer requires every other layer to perform that layer’s job.
The application must know every physical signaling detail.
Layering works only when the physical medium never changes.
understanding.explain: A browser can keep requesting pages after you switch from Ethernet to Wi-Fi because the lower-layer delivery details can change without changing the web request format.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Think of dividing a group project into jobs: each person can improve their part without rewriting everyone else's work.

understanding.q: In the guide’s five-layer TCP/IP stack, which layer lies directly between Transport and Data Link?
options: Network / IP
Transport
Data Link
Physical
understanding.explain: Top to bottom is Application → Transport → Network/IP → Data Link → Physical. Presentation is part of the seven-layer OSI model.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: A question asks how to reach the next device on the local link, using a MAC address. Which layer is responsible?
options: Data Link
Transport
Physical
Network / IP
understanding.explain: Data Link handles frames and local MAC addressing. Network/IP addresses the different problem of routing across networks.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: Two companies want their networking products to work together. What goal of the OSI model supports this?
understanding.answer: A shared model for standardizing communication functions
options: A shared model for standardizing communication functions
Requiring every vendor to implement one inseparable networking layer
Defining different incompatible functions for each manufacturer
Providing only cable specifications rather than a model of communication
understanding.explain: A common seven-job reference helps people compare network designs and locate faults even when vendors build different products.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: OSI is a map of responsibilities, not seven physical boxes inside a computer.

understanding.q: Formatting and compressing data are separated from starting and ending sessions. Which OSI layer handles formatting and compression?
options: Presentation
Session
Application
Transport
understanding.explain: A receiver needs to interpret a sender's representation of data. The OSI Presentation role covers format translation and concepts such as compression and encryption.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Changing how information is represented is different from choosing the route it travels.

understanding.q: A group is developing an Ethernet LAN standard. Which organization in the guide is the relevant standards authority?
options: IEEE
IETF, because it specifically develops Ethernet LAN standards
A regional registry, because it specifies Ethernet framing
IEEE and IETF have no role in any networking standards
understanding.explain: The guide associates IEEE with LAN/WLAN standards such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi. It associates IETF with Internet protocols such as TCP/IP, DNS and HTTP.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: A device turns a sequence of bits into light pulses on a cable. Which layer’s main responsibility is being performed?
options: Physical
Data Link, because it sends complete MAC frames
Network, because it decides the destination route
Transport, because it provides end-to-end process communication
understanding.explain: A bit is an idea, not something a receiver can directly sense. The sender represents bits using voltage, light or radio so the receiver can measure them.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Copper carries electrical signals; fiber carries light; wireless uses radio.

understanding.q: Which item is the medium carrying a signal, rather than an address or a networking model?
options: Copper cable
The frame structure that organizes the carried bits
The signal’s frequency rather than its transmission path
The addressing scheme used by the endpoints
understanding.explain: A signal needs somewhere to travel. Copper, optical fiber and radio space provide different paths with different distance and interference limits.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Separate the path from the message: a cable is the medium; voltage changes are the signal.

understanding.q: A material can carry a signal across a desk but not across the required building distance. Why might it be unsuitable?
understanding.answer: It does not meet the required distance for the link.
options: It does not meet the required distance for the link.
Distance does not matter once the material can carry any signal.
Bandwidth automatically stays constant at every distance.
A medium needs only to be easy to install, not to carry the required link.
understanding.explain: Suitability depends on the actual link requirements: speed, distance, interference resistance, reliability and installation practicality.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: A link must cover a long distance through an area with strong electromagnetic interference. Which choice best fits the guide’s comparison?
options: Optical fiber
Copper because twisting makes it completely immune to electromagnetic interference
Copper because fiber is useful only for shorter links than copper
Either medium because distance and interference never affect the choice
understanding.explain: A transmitter launches light into fiber and a receiver detects it. Because information is carried optically, electromagnetic interference does not induce electrical noise in the glass.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Think light through glass, not electricity through copper.

understanding.q: If light repeatedly escaped from the core of an optical fiber, which useful process would not be doing its job?
options: Total internal reflection
Light amplification by escaping from the core
Converting light into current at each reflection
Absorbing the light at the core boundary
understanding.explain: At a suitable angle, light traveling in the higher-index core reflects at the lower-index cladding boundary instead of escaping. That helps guide it along the fiber.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: The angle and the two materials matter; not every ray hitting any surface stays inside.

understanding.q: One fiber has a very small core and another has a larger core. Which choice best matches the guide’s long-distance preference?
understanding.answer: Single-mode fiber with the smaller core
options: Single-mode fiber with the smaller core
Multimode fiber because a larger core always means a longer reach
Either type because core size can never affect light propagation
Single-mode because its core is larger than multimode’s core
understanding.explain: A small core supports one spatial propagation mode, avoiding the multiple-path spreading associated with multimode fiber. Suitable optics make long links possible.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: One mode means less spreading from different paths, not an automatic fixed distance for every link.

understanding.q: Why can a sender not simply put abstract 0s and 1s onto a cable without representing them physically?
understanding.answer: The medium carries detectable signals, so bits must be encoded as signals.
options: The medium carries detectable signals, so bits must be encoded as signals.
Only decimal data can be represented by a physical signal.
Binary data already travels without any physical carrier.
Signal conversion is needed only for addresses, never for payload data.
understanding.explain: The receiver must detect a physical change, such as an electrical signal or light pulse, to recover the data values.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: A signal carries lots of data but is difficult to distinguish from noise. Which required property is missing?
options: Reliable detectability and noise resistance
Noise resistance is unnecessary if the bit rate is high.
A good signal should consume more bandwidth even if it carries no more data.
A signal need only be detectable at the sender, not at the receiver.
understanding.explain: Bandwidth efficiency alone is not enough. A good signal must also be detectable and resist noise so the receiver can recover the information.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: A modulation method changes both a wave’s amplitude and phase to carry more bits. Which method is it?
options: QAM
Amplitude modulation alone
Phase modulation alone
Frequency modulation alone
understanding.explain: Combining amplitude and phase creates multiple distinguishable symbol states. More states can carry more bits per symbol, but closer states require cleaner reception.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: More choices per symbol give more information, but make neighboring choices easier for noise to confuse.

understanding.q: Several users share a medium, each taking a separate time slot. What is this, and how would FDM differ?
understanding.answer: TDM; FDM assigns separate frequency ranges.
options: TDM; FDM assigns separate frequency ranges.
FDM; TDM assigns separate frequency ranges.
TDM; FDM also assigns time slots, with no frequency separation.
FDM; both methods require a separate physical cable for every user.
understanding.explain: TDM divides access by time. FDM divides the available frequency range so signals can occupy different bands.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: A component forms frames, checks transmission errors and manages access to a local medium. Which layer best matches these jobs?
options: Data Link
Physical, because framing and MAC addressing are physical-layer jobs
Network/IP, because all local frames are routing-table entries
Transport, because it defines all local MAC addresses
understanding.explain: A local-link receiver needs addressing and error-check information around the carried data. That header/payload/trailer unit is the frame.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: An IP packet can be the contents of an Ethernet frame.

understanding.q: A host has an Ethernet cable available but needs hardware that allows it to connect and has a MAC address. What is needed?
options: A NIC
Only a cable, because the cable itself provides the host’s MAC interface
Only a switch port, with no interface hardware at the host
Only a routing table, which replaces the host’s physical network interface
understanding.explain: A host needs an interface that can transmit and receive using the link technology. The NIC provides that connection rather than choosing Internet routes for every remote network.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: NIC is the computer's network doorway, not the entire network.

understanding.q: A sender needs to reach every device on its local Ethernet network because it does not know which one should respond. Which transmission fits?
options: Broadcast
A frame sent only to one already-known receiver
A frame guaranteed to reach every network on the Internet
A frame sent only to the local switch without reaching other hosts
understanding.explain: One local message may need to reach everyone in a broadcast domain, for example during discovery. Routers normally stop Ethernet broadcasts from spreading into other networks.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Everyone locally is different from everyone on the Internet.

understanding.q: Two devices on traditional shared Ethernet transmit at the same time and detect a collision. What should happen next?
understanding.answer: Stop, wait before retrying, then attempt transmission again.
options: Stop, wait before retrying, then attempt transmission again.
Immediately retry together without waiting.
Continue the same transmissions without stopping.
Wait only before the first transmission, but never after a collision.
understanding.explain: On shared half-duplex Ethernet, simultaneous starts can collide even after listening. Detecting a collision and waiting different random times lets devices retry.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Listen, send, detect collision, stop, wait randomly, retry. Full-duplex switched links do not use this collision procedure.

understanding.q: A student calls 1500 bytes the size of the entire ordinary untagged Ethernet frame. What did the student leave out?
options: The 14-byte header and 4-byte FCS
Only the 8-byte preamble/SFD, because the header and FCS are already included
Only the 14-byte header, because ordinary frames contain no FCS
Only the 4-byte FCS, because 1500 already counts the header
understanding.explain: 1500 bytes is the payload. Adding 14 bytes of header and 4 bytes of FCS gives 1518 bytes. Preamble/SFD is excluded from that count.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide

understanding.q: A frame arrives with corrupted data. Which Ethernet field is used to detect that corruption?
options: FCS
Preamble/SFD
Length/Type
Destination address
understanding.explain: The sender computes a check value over the frame and includes it at the end. A receiver compares its own calculation to detect corruption.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: A mismatch signals damage; the check itself does not repair the data.

understanding.q: In the guide’s traditional MAC-address structure, the first half identifies the manufacturer allocation. How many bits remain for the interface-specific half?
options: 24 bits
48 bits
32 bits
16 bits
understanding.explain: In a traditional universally assigned MAC address, the first three byte pairs identify an IEEE-assigned organization prefix. The remaining part is assigned within that block.
understanding.note: Check your understanding · Based on your guide
understanding.remember: Remember: Three bytes × eight bits = 24 bits. Locally assigned MAC addresses need not identify a manufacturer.

understanding.q: Which decimal value equals the binary number 00001101?
understanding.explain: The 1s are in the 8, 4 and 1 positions. Add them: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. Do not read binary digits as a decimal number.

understanding.q: A device knows which port leads to a particular destination MAC and sends a known-destination frame to that port. Is it acting like a hub or a switch?

The physical signal layer converting bits into voltage
The OSI layer that manages application sessions
Access layer: The high-speed backbone tier linking major distribution areas
The tier whose primary job is aggregating several access networks
The OSI layer that formats and encrypts data
Backbone: The cable from a network room to a single user desk only
The final host bits in an IP address
The manufacturer half of a MAC address
Enterprise network: Only a single Ethernet collision domain, never multiple locations
Only one building’s horizontal cabling by definition
A regional registry’s allocation rules, not an organization’s network
Firewall: A system that forwards every packet without any traffic policy
A physical signal generator that replaces routing
A protocol that assigns manufacturers their OUI
Authentication: Deciding whether traffic is electrically detectable
Assigning each packet a new cable category
Measuring network speed without verifying identity
Network maintenance: Only initial requirements analysis before any network exists
Only the one-time installation, with no ongoing monitoring
Waiting for complete failure instead of testing or updating
Downtime: A period when every service is available and functioning normally
The maximum link rate measured in bits per second
The number of host addresses within a prefix
Polling: A device sending an unsolicited notification without a manager’s request
A manager permanently disabling all device measurements
A switch learning MAC addresses solely from Ethernet frames
SNMP agent: The central manager that sends every request to other devices
The cable carrying raw bits between two hosts
SNMP trap: A scheduled request from the manager asking for a reading
A response that can occur only after a polling request
A protocol that blocks all redundant Ethernet links
Standard: A vendor-specific rule intended to prevent interoperability
A transient temperature value from one device
A random configuration selected without review or agreement
Working group: A set of hosts that happen to share the same last IP octet
A fixed route through a series of routers
A group dedicated only to measuring cable lengths after installation

notes.title: The big picture: one message, several jobs
notes.body:
Imagine sending a letter across the world. You write the letter (**Application**), put it in an envelope addressed to a specific person (**Transport**), add a street address and zip code so the post office can route it (**Network**), hand it to a mail truck operating on a local street (**Data Link**), and the truck moves physically across paved roads (**Physical**). 

Computer networking uses this exact divided approach called **Layering**. Instead of building one giant system that handles everything from web page code down to copper electricity, the process is divided into separate, independent layers.
notes.remember: Remember: Each layer does one part of delivery. The letter analogy is a memory aid, not an exact description of every protocol.

notes.title: What is Layering & Why is it Used?
notes.body:
* **Layering** means dividing the complex task of networking into separate, stacked levels, where each level has one specific job.
* **Why it’s useful**:
  1. **Modularity / Layer Independence**: You can upgrade or change one layer (e.g., changing the local connection from Wi-Fi to Ethernet, which changes Physical and Data Link details) without redesigning your web browser at the Application layer.
  2. **Simplicity & Troubleshooting**: It breaks a massive problem into manageable parts, making it easy to isolate where a network failure is happening.
  3. **Standardization**: Allows hardware and software from hundreds of different vendors to work together seamlessly.
notes.remember: Remember: Each layer has its own job. You can investigate one job without having to understand the whole network at once.

notes.title: The TCP/IP Model (How the Internet Actually Works)
notes.body:
Your course teaches a **five-layer TCP/IP model**. Other references group Data Link and Physical into one Link layer and therefore show four. Use five for this guide.

| Layer # | Layer Name | Primary Function | Key Data Unit (PDU) | Key Address Type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **5** | **Application** | Provides network services directly to end-user software (e.g., web browsers, email clients). | Data / Message | Domain Names / URLs |
| **4** | **Transport** | Manages end-to-end communication between applications; handles segmentation, reassembly, and port numbers. | Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) | Port Numbers (e.g., Port 80 for HTTP) |
| **3** | **Network (IP)** | Handles logical IP addressing and routes packets across multiple interconnected networks. | IP Packet | IP Address (e.g., `173.245.63.1`) |
| **2** | **Data Link** | Transfers frames across a single local link/hop between adjacent devices using physical hardware addresses. | Frame | MAC Address (e.g., `00-15-C5-57-1D-1A`) |
| **1** | **Physical** | Transmits raw binary bits (0s and 1s) as electrical voltage, light pulses, or radio waves over a medium. | Bits | None |
notes.remember: Remember: Think top to bottom: application data, transport delivery, IP routing, local frames, then physical signals.

notes.title: The OSI Model (The Theoretical Blueprint)
notes.body:
* **OSI Model (Open Systems Interconnection)**: A 7-layer reference model developed to standardize networking so equipment from any vendor could interoperate. While TCP/IP is what we actually use, OSI is the standard theoretical blueprint.
* **The 7 Layers (Top-to-Bottom)**:
  1. **Application**: Network services for software.
  2. **Presentation**: Data formatting, compression, and encryption/decryption.
  3. **Session**: Establishes, manages, and terminates communication sessions between hosts.
  4. **Transport**: End-to-end communication between application processes. TCP adds reliable delivery and flow control; not every transport protocol guarantees these.
  5. **Network**: IP addressing and global routing.
  6. **Data Link**: Local node-to-node framing and error detection.
  7. **Physical**: Hardware signaling and bit transmission.
* **Mnemonic to Remember 7 to 1**: **A**ll **P**eople **S**eem **T**o **N**eed **D**ata **P**rocessing.
* **Mnemonic to Remember 1 to 7**: **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way.
notes.remember: Remember: OSI separates seven jobs. Presentation changes the data’s format; Session manages the conversation.

notes.title: Encapsulation vs. Decapsulation
notes.body:
* **Encapsulation (Sending side)**: The process of wrapping data in headers (and sometimes trailers) as it moves down through the layers.
  * *Analogy*: You write a letter (**Data**), put it in a box (**TCP Segment**), place that box inside an Amazon brown box with an IP shipping label (**IP Packet**), and load that box onto a delivery truck (**Ethernet Frame**).
* **Decapsulation (Receiving side)**: The reverse process where the receiving device strips off headers layer by layer as data moves up the stack.
* **Remember**: A router removes the incoming link-layer frame and builds a new frame for the next link. Ordinary switches do not rewrite the frame at every switch hop. IP source and destination addresses usually remain the same without address translation, but IP headers are not completely unchanged: routers reduce TTL and update the IPv4 header checksum.
notes.remember: Remember: Sending adds wrapping; receiving removes it. A router builds new link-layer wrapping for the next link.

notes.title: Vocabulary: Computer Network Authorities
notes.body:
Standards ensure devices worldwide speak the same language:
* **IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)**: *"Cables & Wi-Fi people."* Sets LAN and physical/data-link standards (e.g., Ethernet = `IEEE 802.3`, Wi-Fi = `IEEE 802.11`).
* **IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force)**: *"Internet protocol people."* Creates TCP/IP stack standards like HTTP, TCP, IP, and DNS.
* **ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers)**: *"Domain names boss."* Coordinates the global domain-name system and root-zone policy; it does not operate every DNS root server.
* **IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority)**: *"Numbers and ports clerk."* Coordinates global IP-number resources and protocol-parameter registries, including port numbers. The IANA functions are performed by Public Technical Identifiers, an ICANN affiliate; regional registries handle regional allocations.
* **ITU (International Telecommunication Union)**: *"Global telecom referee."* UN agency that sets global WAN and carrier telecom standards.
* **TIA (Telecommunications Industry Association)**: *"Building cabling people."* Writes commercial cabling standards (e.g., TIA-568) for building wiring.
notes.remember: Remember: IEEE is the Ethernet/Wi-Fi standards group; IETF is the Internet-protocol standards group.

notes.title: Primary Responsibility & Physical Media
notes.body:
* **Primary Function**: To convert raw binary bits (0s and 1s) into physical signals (electricity, light, radio waves) and send them through a medium.
* **Physical Medium**: The physical path that carries a signal between devices.
* **Required Properties of a Good Medium**: Must effectively conduct signals, support required data rates (bandwidth), transmit over desired distances, resist environmental noise/interference, and be cost-effective to install.
notes.remember: Remember: Bits are information. Signals are the physical form that lets those bits travel.

notes.title: Copper Cabling: UTP Categories
notes.body:
* **UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair)**: Copper cabling containing pairs of insulated wires twisted around each other. 
  * **Why twist the wires?** Twisting helps reduce electromagnetic interference (EMI) and crosstalk between pairs. Cable performance depends on the complete cable design and installation, not only how tightly it is twisted.
  * **STP (Shielded Twisted Pair)**: Includes an extra foil shield around wires for high-noise industrial environments.
* **Twisted-pair cable categories and common Ethernet limits** (Cat 8 is shielded, not UTP):
  * **Cat 5e (Enhanced)**: Up to **1 Gbps** (Gigabit Ethernet).
  * **Cat 6**: Up to **1 Gbps** (and 10 Gbps over short distances up to 55m).
  * **Cat 6a (Augmented)**: Full **10 Gbps** up to 100 meters.
  * **Cat 8**: **25 Gbps to 40 Gbps** over short distances (30m, ideal for Data Centers).
* **Baseband vs. Broadband**:
  * **Baseband**: Uses the entire cable bandwidth to transmit **one single digital signal** at a time (e.g., Ethernet).
  * **Broadband**: Divides cable bandwidth into multiple channels to send **multiple signals simultaneously** (e.g., Cable TV).
notes.remember: Remember: Twists reduce interference. Choose cable by the required speed and distance, not just its category number.

notes.title: Fiber Optics: Single-Mode vs. Multi-Mode
notes.body:
**Optical fiber** is a thin strand of glass that conducts light using **Total Internal Reflection**. Light strikes the boundary between the inner core and outer cladding at an angle greater than the critical angle, trapping the light inside the core so it travels vast distances without escaping.

Why is Fiber better than Copper? Fiber can support high bandwidth and long links and is immune to electromagnetic interference. Reach still depends on the fiber, optics and data rate; sufficiently long links need amplification or regeneration.

| Feature | Single-Mode Fiber (SMF) | Multi-Mode Fiber (MMF) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Diameter** | Very small (**9 µm**) | Larger (**50 – 62.5 µm**) |
| **Light Source** | Laser | LED or laser, including VCSELs in many modern links |
| **Distance** | **Very Long Distances** (miles/km across cities/oceans) | **Short Distances** (inside a building or data center) |
| **Cost** | More expensive optics/transceivers | Lower cost optics |
notes.remember: Remember: A fiber guides light through its core. Single-mode usually suits longer links; multimode usually suits shorter ones.

notes.title: Signaling & Modulation
notes.body:
Computers cannot transmit abstract concepts of 0 and 1 directly; they must convert binary data into physical signals.

* **Properties of a Good Signal**: Easily detectable by receiver, resistant to noise, bandwidth efficient, and supports multiplexing.
* **Modulation Types**:
  * **AM (Amplitude Modulation)**: Varies the height/strength of the wave. Simple, but highly sensitive to noise.
  * **FM (Frequency Modulation)**: Varies the frequency (cycles per second) of the wave. Good noise resistance.
  * **PM (Phase Modulation)**: Varies the starting position/angle (phase) of the wave.
  * **QAM (Quadrature Amplitude Modulation)**: Combines **AM + PM** simultaneously. It packs multiple bits into every signal state, making it extremely **bandwidth efficient** (used in Wi-Fi and 5G), but higher-order QAM is sensitive to channel noise.
notes.remember: Remember: Amplitude means wave strength, frequency means cycles per second, and phase means position in the cycle. QAM changes amplitude and phase together.

notes.title: Mathematical Limits & Multiplexing
notes.body:
* **Shannon-Hartley Theorem**: Calculates the theoretical capacity for a bandwidth-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise (Channel Capacity C in bits per second) over a noisy channel:
**C = B × log₂(1 + S/N)**
  * B = Channel Bandwidth in Hertz (Hz).
  * S/N = Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), expressed as a linear power ratio, not decibels.
  * *Takeaway*: Higher bandwidth (B) or cleaner signals (higher S/N) yield higher data capacity (C).

* **Multiplexing**: Combining multiple separate signals onto a single shared physical medium to save cabling costs.
  * **FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing)**: Divides the channel into different **frequency bands** (like tuning radio stations or low/high pitches). Separates signals by frequency; those carriers can carry analog or digital information.
  * **TDM (Time Division Multiplexing)**: Devices take **turns in time slots** to send data over the full frequency. Common in digital systems; its defining feature is division by time.
notes.remember: Remember: Multiplexing lets several conversations share one medium. FDM separates frequencies; TDM separates turns in time.

notes.title: Primary Functions of Data Link Layer
notes.body: Operating across a single local link/hop, the Data Link layer creates **Frames**, handles hardware addressing (**MAC addresses**), detects transmission errors (**CRC**), and regulates media access (**CSMA/CD**).
notes.remember: Remember: Data Link organizes local delivery into frames. Physical carries the signals underneath those frames.

notes.title: Ethernet Operation & CSMA/CD
notes.body:
On traditional shared Ethernet, other connected interfaces can hear a transmission. A unicast frame is addressed to one interface; an Ethernet broadcast frame is addressed to all interfaces in the broadcast domain. Modern switched Ethernet does not send every known unicast frame to every workstation.

When multiple devices share a medium, they can transmit at the same time, causing a **Collision**. This applies to shared half-duplex Ethernet; modern full-duplex switched links do not use CSMA/CD. Shared Ethernet resolves this using **CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection)**:
1. **Carrier Sense**: Listen to the wire first ("listen before speaking").
2. **Multiple Access**: If the wire is quiet, transmit.
3. **Collision Detect**: If two devices transmit simultaneously, they detect the voltage spike collision.
4. **Backoff**: Both devices immediately stop, send a jam signal, wait a random fraction of a second (exponential backoff), and retransmit.
notes.remember: Remember: Listen first. If a collision happens on a shared half-duplex link, stop, signal the collision, wait a random time and retry.

notes.title: Ethernet Frame Structure & Math
notes.body:
The maximum **ordinary untagged Ethernet frame** in this guide is **1,518 bytes**; tagged and jumbo frames differ (excluding the 8-byte Preamble and Start Frame Delimiter):

**1518 bytes = 14-byte header + 1500-byte payload + 4-byte FCS**

* **Preamble + SFD (8 Bytes)**: Synchronizes clock timing between sender and receiver.
* **Destination MAC Address (6 Bytes / 48 bits)**: Physical address of receiving device.
* **Source MAC Address (6 Bytes / 48 bits)**: Physical address of sending device.
* **Type/Length (2 Bytes)**: Identifies the layer-3 protocol inside (e.g., IPv4).
* **Payload Data**: The encapsulated IP packet (46 to 1500 Bytes).
* **FCS (Frame Check Sequence - 4 Bytes)**: Contains a **CRC-32 (Cyclic Redundancy Check)** used to detect corruption. A failed check indicates an error. A passing check means no error was detected, not proof that every bit must be correct.
notes.remember: Remember: For an ordinary untagged frame: 14 + 1500 + 4 = 1518 bytes. The preamble and SFD are outside that count.

notes.title: MAC Address Structure & Hexadecimal Conversions
notes.body:
A traditional Ethernet **MAC address** is 48 bits (6 bytes). Interfaces often have a factory-assigned address, but software can also set or randomize MAC addresses; they are not necessarily permanent.
* **First 24 bits**: **OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier)**—assigned by IEEE to the manufacturer (e.g., Cisco, Broadcom).
* **Last 24 bits**: Unique extension/serial number assigned by the manufacturer.

#### Number Conversion Practice for the Exam:
1. **Binary to Decimal**: Sum the positional powers of 2 (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1) where a 1 appears:
**10101101₂ = 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173₁₀**
2. **Binary to Hexadecimal**: Group the 8 bits into two 4-bit nibbles (8, 4, 2, 1):
**1010 1111₂ → 1010 = A and 1111 = F → AF₁₆**
notes.remember: Remember: A MAC address has six bytes. For number conversions, add binary place values or group bits into fours for hex.

notes.title: Network Hardware & Topologies
notes.body:
* **Hub vs. Switch**:
  * **Hub (Layer 1)**: Dumb multiport repeater. A signal received on one port is repeated to the other ports. Creates a single large collision domain.
  * **Switch (Layer 2)**: Intelligent device. Reads incoming Source MAC addresses to dynamically build a **MAC Address Table** (`[MAC Address → Switch Port]`). For a known unicast destination, forwards to the learned destination port. Broadcasts and unknown unicasts are flooded to other eligible ports in the same VLAN.
* **Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)**:
  * **Problem**: Redundant links between switches create switching **loops**, causing frames to circulate endlessly and crash the network.
  * **Solution**: Invented by **Radia Perlman**, STP dynamically blocks redundant paths to create a single loop-free tree structure, automatically unblocking backup paths if a link fails.
* **Topologies**:
  * **Star**: All devices connect to a central switch. **Dominant topology today** because it offers superior fault tolerance, easy maintenance, and security.
  * **Bus**: Single central backbone cable with terminators at both ends.
  * **Ring**: Devices connected in a closed circle.
  * **Mesh**: Devices have redundant connections to each other (Full Mesh or Partial Mesh).
notes.remember: Remember: A hub repeats signals. A switch learns which MAC addresses are on which ports. STP prevents loops when switches have redundant links.

notes.title: Why do we need IP Addresses when we already have MAC Addresses?
notes.body:
* **MAC Address (Layer 2)**: Link-layer interface address; often factory-assigned but not necessarily permanent. It only works for **local hop-by-hop delivery** within a single network segment.
* **IP Address (Layer 3)**: Logical, hierarchical address that identifies the device’s network location for routing, not its physical geographic location across interconnected networks.
* **Layering Independence**: Allows you to replace a network card (changing the MAC address) without changing the computer's logical IP address or server configurations.
notes.remember: Remember: MAC helps with the next local delivery. IP helps routers choose a path across networks.

notes.title: IP Address Structure & Math Rules
notes.body:
An IPv4 address consists of **32 bits** divided into two parts: `[Network Portion | Host Portion]`.

#### Exam Math Problems:
1. **How many objects can be labeled with n bits?**
**Number of unique labels = 2ⁿ**
   * *Example*: With 10 bits, 2^10 = 1,024 unique objects can be labeled.
   * *Example*: To label 200 objects, find the smallest power of 2 that covers 200: 2^7 = 128 (too small), 2^8 = 256 (sufficient). Answer = **8 bits**.

2. **CIDR Subnet Calculations (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)**:
   * Classful addressing (Classes A, B, C) was rigid and wasted millions of addresses. CIDR replaced it by allowing variable prefix lengths using slash notation (e.g., `/17`).
   * *Exam Problem*: For network `73.5.0.0/17`:
     * Total IPv4 bits = 32.
     * Network bits = 17.
     * Host bits = 32 - 17 = **15 host bits**.
     * **Total IP Addresses**: 2^15 = **32,768  addresses**.
     * **Usable Host Addresses**: 2^15 - 2 = **32,766  usable hosts**.
     * *(Why subtract 2? We reserve the first address as the Network ID and the last address as the Subnet Broadcast Address)*.

The subtract-two rule is for traditional IPv4 subnets; /31 point-to-point links and /32 host routes are exceptions.
notes.remember: Remember: The slash number tells you how many bits are network bits. Subtract it from 32 to find the IPv4 host bits.

notes.title: IPv4 vs. IPv6
notes.body:
* **IPv4**: **32 bits** long, written in 4 dotted-decimal octets (e.g., `192.168.1.1`). Yields ≈ 4.3  billion addresses, The address space is limited, and new-address allocation is constrained.
* **IPv6**: **128 bits** long, written in hexadecimal separated by colons. Yields 2^128 ≈ 3.4 × 10^38 addresses.
  * **Shortening Rules**:
    1. Omit leading zeros in any 16-bit block (`0011` → `11`, `0db8` → `db8`).
    2. Replace continuous blocks of zeros with a single double-colon `::` **(can only be done ONCE in an address)**.
    * *Example*: `2001:0db8:aaaa:0000:0000:0000:eeee:0001` shortens to `2001:db8:aaaa::eeee:1`.
notes.remember: Remember: IPv4 is 32 bits; IPv6 is 128. In IPv6, :: is a shortcut for consecutive zero groups and can appear only once.

notes.title: Routing, ICMP & IP Registries
notes.body:
* **Routing & Routing Tables**: Routing is the process of forwarding packets across networks. A **Routing Table** stores destination network prefixes, metrics/costs, and the next-hop router address.
* **ICMP Utilities (Internet Control Message Protocol)**: Used for diagnostic messages and status reporting:
  * **Ping**: Tests basic reachability to a target host via Echo Request/Reply.
  * **Traceroute**: Attempts to show successive router hops. Some routers do not reply, and paths can change.
  * **Pathping**: Combines ping and traceroute to measure packet loss and latency at each intermediate hop over time.
* **Regional Internet Registries (RIRs)**: Regional organizations (such as ARIN and RIPE NCC) that manage and distribute public IP address allocations regionally to prevent IP conflicts.
notes.remember: Remember: Ping asks for a reply. Traceroute explores the hops. Regional registries coordinate public address allocations.

notes.title: Network Design Goals & Phases
notes.body:
* **Primary Goal**: Meet current and future end-user needs using appropriate technology while **minimizing total costs** (initial setup + ongoing maintenance + cost of downtime).
* **Requirements Analysis Phase**: Gathering user counts, applications, physical locations, traffic volumes, and security/special device needs.
* **Logical Network Design**: A conceptual drawing/map showing network structure, subnets, IP ranges, device counts (desktops, servers, printers), and services (DNS, DHCP, firewalls) **without specifying vendor brand names**.
* **Physical Network Design**: Translates the logical design into explicit physical hardware specs, media types (Cat6a vs Fiber), specific switch models, and router configurations.
notes.remember: Remember: First learn what users need. Then plan the network, choose equipment and account for ongoing costs.

notes.title: Structured Cabling Components
notes.body:
Building cabling is organized into standardized facilities:
* **Demarc (Demarcation Point)**: The exact physical point where the Telecom ISP’s network ends and the customer’s internal building network begins.
* **MDF (Main Distribution Frame)**: The primary central telecommunications room housing core switches, main patch panels, and ISP handoffs.
* **IDF (Intermediate Distribution Frame)**: Secondary wiring closets located on individual floors that connect local devices and uplink back to the MDF.
* **Horizontal Cabling**: Cabling running from floor telecommunications rooms (IDFs) out to work area wall outlets. **For a typical structured copper channel: 90 meters of permanent cabling + 10 meters of patch cords = 100 meters. Specific standards, including Cat 8, have different limits**.
* **Vertical / Backbone Cabling**: High-capacity backbone links (typically fiber) connecting the MDF across floors to IDFs or adjacent buildings.
notes.remember: Remember: Horizontal goes to work areas; backbone joins telecommunications spaces. MDF is the main distribution point and IDFs serve other areas.

notes.title: Data Center & Campus Architectures
notes.body:
* **Data Center Leaf-Spine Architecture**: Every **Leaf switch** connects to every **Spine switch**. Provides multiple predictable paths between servers. Capacity and whether the network is non-blocking depend on link speeds and oversubscription.
* **Campus 3-Tier Architecture**: Organizes large multi-building networks into three distinct layers:

```
   [ Core Layer ]         <-- High-speed Backbone (fast transport)
         |
[ Distribution Layer ]    <-- Policy, Routing between VLANs, Firewalls
         |
  [ Access Layer ]        <-- Connects End-User PCs & Workstations
```

1. **Core Layer**: The fast network backbone. Prioritizes fast, reliable transport between distribution blocks; exact policy placement depends on the design.
2. **Distribution Layer**: Aggregates access networks and commonly handles inter-subnet routing and policy. Firewalls, authentication and QoS placement depend on the design.
3. **Access Layer**: Provides work-area ports to end users; contains user switches/hubs organizing building devices into local network segments.
* **Enterprise Network**: Connects geographically scattered campus networks over Wide Area Networks (WANs) managed by service providers.
notes.remember: Remember: Access connects users, Distribution brings access networks together, and Core provides the fast backbone.

notes.title: Network Maintenance & SNMP
notes.body:
* **Maintenance Activities**: Ongoing inspection, testing, hardware replacement, and software patching to maintain service availability. Vulnerability tools such as **Nessus** can help identify missing patches and other issues; they do not replace the patching process.
* **SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)**: A protocol that allows a central Management Station to monitor and control network hardware remotely:
  * **Agent**: Software running inside routers, switches, and servers.
  * **MIB (Management Information Base)**: A structured definition of managed objects, such as counters and temperature readings. An agent exposes the actual values; the MIB describes what those objects mean.
  * **GET Command**: Management station asks the agent for managed-object values to retrieve statistics (e.g., CPU usage, toner percentage).
  * **SET Command**: Management station asks the agent to change an authorized writable managed object (e.g., shutting down a port, changing routing).
notes.remember: Remember: The manager asks; the agent answers. The MIB describes the information available through SNMP.

notes.title: Standards Development Process
notes.body:
How standard protocols (like Wi-Fi `802.11ax` or `TCP/IP`) are created:
1. An expert lead organization (like IEEE or IETF) identifies a industry need and forms a Working Group.
2. Requirements are published.
3. Technology companies submit proposed solutions.
4. Proposals undergo technical review, revision and approval. Procedures differ: IEEE uses ballots, while IETF working groups seek rough consensus rather than a simple majority vote.
notes.remember: Remember: A standard is a shared rule. Experts propose, discuss, revise and approve it so different products can work together.

notes.title: Binary → decimal · step by step
notes.body:
#### Start with the names
Chapter 3 uses binary and hexadecimal to understand MAC addresses. Chapter 4 uses binary for IP addresses. Decimal is the ordinary counting system you already use: 0, 1, 2 … 10 … 173. Binary writes the same quantities using only 0 and 1. Converting changes how we write a number, not its size.

#### Each position has a value
A bit is one binary digit: either 0 or 1. In an eight-bit number, the positions are worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 from left to right. Start at 1 on the RIGHT and double each time you move left. These values are fixed; do not rearrange them.

#### Line up the digits
Example: 10101101.
Place values: 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1
Binary digits:     1 |  0 |  1 |  0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1
A 1 means “include this value.” A 0 means “skip this value.” Think of each digit as an on/off switch for the value above it.

#### Add only the switched-on values
For 10101101, include 128, skip 64, include 32, skip 16, include 8, include 4, skip 2, include 1.
128 + 32 = 160
160 + 8 = 168
168 + 4 = 172
172 + 1 = 173
So 10101101 in binary is 173 in decimal. Do not count the 1s; add their POSITION values.

#### One smaller example
00000101 means 4 + 1 = 5. The zeros at the beginning do not add anything. That is why 101 and 00000101 have the same value. In networking we often keep all eight bits to show one byte clearly.
notes.remember: Remember: 00000101 means 4 + 1 = 5. The zeros at the beginning do not add anything. That is why 101 and 00000101 have the same value. In networking we often keep all eight bits to show one byte clearly.

notes.title: Decimal → binary · step by step
notes.body:
#### What are we trying to build?
We want to write the ordinary number 173 using only 0s and 1s. For a number from 0 through 255, use eight positions: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Think of picking value cards that add up to 173.

#### The rule: can this value fit?
Start with a remaining amount of 173. Move from the biggest position to the smallest. If its value fits in the remaining amount, write 1 and subtract it. If it is too big, write 0 and keep the remaining amount. Write one digit for EVERY position.

#### Build the first four digits
128 fits in 173 → write 1; 173 − 128 = 45 left.
64 is too big for 45 → write 0; still 45 left.
32 fits in 45 → write 1; 45 − 32 = 13 left.
16 is too big for 13 → write 0; still 13 left.
So far: 1010.

#### Finish the last four digits
8 fits in 13 → write 1; 13 − 8 = 5 left.
4 fits in 5 → write 1; 5 − 4 = 1 left.
2 is too big for 1 → write 0; still 1 left.
1 fits in 1 → write 1; 1 − 1 = 0 left.
Last four digits: 1101. Together: 10101101.

#### Check your work
Read the 1 positions back: 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173. You got the starting number back, so your conversion works. If the remaining amount reaches zero early, fill every remaining position with 0.
notes.remember: Remember: Read the 1 positions back: 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173. You got the starting number back, so your conversion works. If the remaining amount reaches zero early, fill every remaining position with 0.

notes.title: Hexadecimal → binary · step by step
notes.body:
#### Why are there letters in a number?
Hexadecimal, or hex, has 16 digit symbols. After 0–9 it uses A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. These letters are number digits here. MAC addresses use hex because it is shorter to read than a long string of bits.

#### One hex digit becomes four bits
Four binary positions have values 8, 4, 2, 1. They can represent 0 through 15, exactly the values of one hex digit. So EVERY hex digit becomes exactly four bits, including zeros at the beginning.

#### Convert A first
Example: AF. Take A by itself. A means 10.
8 fits in 10 → 1; 2 left.
4 is too big → 0.
2 fits → 1; 0 left.
1 does not fit → 0.
A becomes 1010.

#### Convert F, then join
F means 15. 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15, so all four positions are on: 1111.
A → 1010
F → 1111
Keep the original order and join: AF → 10101111. Do not add the two groups together.

#### Keep all four bits for each digit
For 05: 0 becomes 0000 and 5 becomes 0101. Join them to get 00000101. Writing 5 as just 101 would lose the four-bit grouping that makes hex easy to read.
notes.remember: Remember: For 05: 0 becomes 0000 and 5 becomes 0101. Join them to get 00000101. Writing 5 as just 101 would lose the four-bit grouping that makes hex easy to read.

notes.title: Binary → hexadecimal · step by step
notes.body:
#### Make groups of four
Hex is a shorter way to write binary. Start at the RIGHT and split the bits into groups of four. Example: 10101111 becomes 1010 | 1111. Each group becomes ONE hex digit.

#### Give each group its own values
Inside every four-bit group, the values are 8, 4, 2, 1. Start over with those values for the next group. Do not use 128, 64, 32, 16 for the first group when converting directly to hex.

#### Convert the first group
1010 uses the 8 position and the 2 position.
8 + 2 = 10.
Hex uses A for 10, so 1010 becomes A.
Remember the letter values: A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.

#### Convert the second group and join
1111 uses all four positions.
8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 → F.
First group A, second group F: the answer is AF. Preserve the order; AF and FA are different numbers.

#### What if there are fewer than four bits?
Add zeros to the LEFT until the leftmost group has four bits. Example: 101 becomes 0101 → 4 + 1 = 5 → hex 5. Adding zeros to the right would change the number, so only pad on the left.
notes.remember: Remember: Add zeros to the LEFT until the leftmost group has four bits. Example: 101 becomes 0101 → 4 + 1 = 5 → hex 5. Adding zeros to the right would change the number, so only pad on the left.

notes.title: Hexadecimal → decimal · step by step
notes.body:
#### Hex digits have positions too
In decimal, 23 means 2 tens plus 3 ones. In a two-digit hex number, the left digit counts groups of SIXTEEN and the right digit counts ones. Hex place values from right to left are 1, 16, 256, 4096. Each step left multiplies the place value by 16.

#### Translate letters into values
Example: AF. A means 10 and F means 15. Do not add 10 + 15 yet: the A is in the sixteens position, so its position matters.

#### Multiply by the position, then add
A in the sixteens position: 10 × 16 = 160.
F in the ones position: 15 × 1 = 15.
160 + 15 = 175.
So AF in hex is 175 in decimal.

#### Try a number without letters
Hex 20 means 2 × 16 + 0 × 1 = 32 in decimal. It does NOT mean decimal twenty. Always check which number system the question names. You may also see hex written as 0x20; 0x is a label meaning hexadecimal.
notes.remember: Remember: Hex 20 means 2 × 16 + 0 × 1 = 32 in decimal. It does NOT mean decimal twenty. Always check which number system the question names. You may also see hex written as 0x20; 0x is a label meaning hexadecimal.

notes.title: Decimal → hexadecimal · step by step
notes.body:
#### Use groups of sixteen
For the byte-sized values used here (0–255), ask: how many full groups of 16 fit in the decimal number, and how many ones are left over? The group count becomes the left hex digit. The leftover amount becomes the right digit.

#### Find the full groups
Example: 175.
10 × 16 = 160 fits.
11 × 16 = 176 is too much.
So 175 contains 10 full groups of 16.
175 − 160 = 15 left over. This leftover is called the remainder.

#### Turn both values into hex digits
The group count is 10 → A.
The remainder is 15 → F.
Write the group digit first, then the remainder digit: AF.
Check: 10 × 16 + 15 = 175.

#### A smaller example and another route
Decimal 35 contains 2 groups of 16, with 3 left over: 35 − 32 = 3. So it becomes hex 23. For a full byte, decimal 5 is hex 05. You can also convert decimal → eight-bit binary → two four-bit groups → hex if that method feels easier.
notes.remember: Remember: Decimal 35 contains 2 groups of 16, with 3 left over: 35 − 32 = 3. So it becomes hex 23. For a full byte, decimal 5 is hex 05. You can also convert decimal → eight-bit binary → two four-bit groups → hex if that method feels easier.

notes.title: Bits, exponents & counting unique labels
notes.body:
A **bit** is a position that can be 0 or 1. With one bit you have two labels: 0 and 1. With two bits you have four: 00, 01, 10, 11. Each extra bit doubles the number of choices.

**2ⁿ** means multiply n factors of 2. The raised n is the exponent. Here n is the number of bits, while the result is the number of different labels.

For 3 bits: 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 labels. For 10 bits: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 labels. This is not 2 × 10.

To label 200 objects, choose the smallest bit count with enough combinations: 2⁷ = 128 is too few; 2⁸ = 256 works. You need 8 bits.

Do not subtract 2 for this task. Reserving network and broadcast addresses is a separate IPv4 subnet rule.
notes.remember: Each extra bit doubles the choices. Bits are positions; labels are combinations.

notes.title: Hop-by-hop vs. end-to-end delivery
notes.body:
#### One journey, two delivery scopes
Chapter 3 explains local frames; Chapter 4 explains IP delivery across networks; Chapter 1 places Transport above IP. Imagine sending a package through several delivery stops. The final destination stays on the inner address label, while each local handoff needs its own outer label.

#### What does “link-layer wrapper” actually mean?
Start with the message you want to send, such as a request for a web page. Your computer prepares an IP packet: a bundle of data that includes the final destination’s IP address.

To carry that packet across a local Ethernet connection, the computer adds information BEFORE it and AFTER it. Think of putting a letter into an envelope. This is only a picture to help you remember: the real envelope is extra bits, not paper.

HEADER = information before the packet. For Ethernet, it includes the source MAC (who sent this local frame), destination MAC (who receives this local frame), and type (what kind of packet is inside).

PAYLOAD = what is inside. In this example, it is the whole IP packet.

TRAILER = information after the packet. Ethernet puts the FCS error check here, helping the receiver detect damage.

FRAME = the whole thing: header + packet inside + trailer. “Link-layer wrapper” means that outer delivery information around the packet. It is another way of describing what the Data Link layer adds.

#### Local-link delivery: the outer frame
On an Ethernet link, the frame has source and destination MAC addresses. For a remote server, your laptop first addresses the frame to its local router, not to the remote server’s MAC address. A local switch can forward that frame without changing its source and destination MAC addresses.

#### At the router: open one envelope, make the next
Imagine your laptop sending a letter to a faraway server. The IP packet inside names that server as the final destination. The first Ethernet envelope is addressed to your local router because that is the next place the laptop can deliver it.

The router receives the frame, checks and removes its local delivery information, and reads the IP destination to choose the next connection. This is what “removes the link-layer wrapper” means: open the current local-delivery envelope and take out the packet.

The router then builds the next link’s frame. On Ethernet, it adds a new header and error-check trailer. The new source MAC belongs to the router’s outgoing interface; the new destination MAC belongs to the next receiver.

The final server is still the IP destination in this example. The outer local label changes because the next delivery stop changes. Assume no NAT here. Other link technologies may use a different frame format.

#### Follow the same message across three links
Assume Ethernet links and ordinary routing with no NAT. Laptop → Router A → Router B → Server. Each routed link uses a different source/destination MAC pair. The source/destination IP addresses still identify the laptop and server. TCP/UDP ports identify their application endpoints. Click each link in the diagram to see which labels change.

#### What end-to-end does—and does not—mean
Transport is process-to-process: it connects application endpoints. IP supplies addressing across networks, but routers still make hop-by-hop forwarding decisions. “Same endpoints” does not mean the whole IP header stays unchanged: routers reduce TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6). NAT may translate IP addresses and, with port translation, ports. For the basic example, assume no NAT.

#### Keep the scope straight
A switch forwarding within one LAN is not the same as a router forwarding onto another IP link. In this lesson, hop-by-hop means local delivery between successive IP forwarding endpoints, not necessarily every physical cable segment. Remember: local MAC label for this leg, IP destination for the wider journey, port for the receiving program.
notes.remember: Local MAC label → this link. IP endpoint → network journey. Port → application endpoint.

notesQuestions.q: Why can a browser keep working when its local connection changes from Wi-Fi to Ethernet?
notesQuestions.answer: Layering separates application services from local-link details.
options: Layering separates application services from local-link details.
Every layer performs exactly the same function.
The browser must use the same radio signals as Ethernet.
Layering removes the need for physical signals.
notesQuestions.explain: The browser still makes the same application-level request. Ethernet and Wi-Fi provide different local delivery methods underneath it, so the browser does not need a new web protocol when the link changes.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Separate the message a program wants to send from the local technology carrying it.

notesQuestions.q: Which information identifies an application endpoint at the Transport layer?
options: Port number
MAC address
IPv4 network prefix
Ethernet FCS
notesQuestions.explain: One computer may run a browser and a mail app together. Transport ports distinguish the application endpoints so incoming data reaches the appropriate conversation.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: An IP address helps reach the device; a port helps reach the program on that device.

notesQuestions.q: Which OSI layer handles data formatting and compression?
options: Presentation
Session
Network
Physical
notesQuestions.explain: A receiver needs to interpret a sender's representation of data. The OSI Presentation role covers format translation and concepts such as compression and encryption.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Representation means the format of information. Session means managing the conversation.

notesQuestions.q: What does a router do with a packet’s link-layer wrapping?
notesQuestions.answer: Removes the received frame and builds a frame for the next link.
options: Removes the received frame and builds a frame for the next link.
Keeps the original link-layer header unchanged through every network.
Removes the IP destination permanently.
Turns the Transport header into a MAC address.
notesQuestions.explain: A link-layer wrapper only serves the current local delivery. At a router, that delivery ends; the router processes the IP packet and creates the appropriate frame for the outgoing link.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: The packet can continue toward the same final IP destination while its next local MAC destination changes.

notesQuestions.q: Which group develops Ethernet and Wi-Fi standards?
options: IEEE
IETF
IANA
ICANN
notesQuestions.explain: IEEE's 802 standards families include wired Ethernet and wireless LAN rules. Shared specifications let interfaces made by different vendors use the same link technology.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Associate IEEE with the local connection: Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

notesQuestions.q: Which organization coordinates the global domain-name system?
options: ICANN
IEEE
TIA
ITU
notesQuestions.explain: The naming system needs coordinated top-level rules and unique identifiers so the same domain name is not delegated inconsistently. ICANN coordinates that global system; ordinary DNS servers answer day-to-day lookups.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Coordinating the naming system is different from personally answering every DNS request.

notesQuestions.q: Which role belongs to IANA?
notesQuestions.answer: Coordinate Internet number resources and protocol-parameter registries.
options: Coordinate Internet number resources and protocol-parameter registries.
Install every organization’s switches.
Write every building’s cabling plan.
Operate every individual DNS server.
notesQuestions.explain: Shared Internet identifiers need coordinated registries. IANA maintains protocol-parameter registries and coordinates global number resources, including allocations to regional registries.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: A registry is an organized record of assigned identifiers; it prevents incompatible assignments.

notesQuestions.q: Which organization is associated with commercial building cabling standards?
options: TIA
IETF
IANA
ICANN
notesQuestions.explain: Building wiring must be installed and organized consistently so links can be tested and maintained. TIA cabling standards address that infrastructure rather than Internet packet-routing rules.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Match the organization to its job: building cabling points to TIA.

notesQuestions.q: Which organization is the UN agency associated with global telecommunications standards?
options: ITU
TIA
IEEE
ARIN
notesQuestions.explain: ITU is a United Nations specialized agency for information and communication technologies; its standardization work helps telecommunications systems operate consistently internationally.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: The United Nations agency clue distinguishes ITU from IEEE and IETF.

notesQuestions.q: What turns an abstract bit into something that travels through a medium?
notesQuestions.answer: Representing it as a physical signal
options: Representing it as a physical signal
Assigning it an application filename
Adding a domain name alone
Recording it in a routing table alone
notesQuestions.explain: A bit is an idea, not something a receiver can directly sense. The sender represents bits using voltage, light or radio so the receiver can measure them.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: The receiver can measure voltage or light; it cannot directly measure the abstract idea of a 0.

notesQuestions.q: Why are copper wire pairs twisted?
notesQuestions.answer: To help reduce interference and crosstalk
options: To help reduce interference and crosstalk
To eliminate every possible transmission error
To turn electrical signals into light
To guarantee the same speed over every distance
notesQuestions.explain: Twisting changes how each conductor is exposed to nearby interference along the cable, helping reduce unwanted coupling and noise in the received differential signal. It does not make copper completely immune to interference.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: The twists help the receiver distinguish the intended signal from unwanted electrical effects.

notesQuestions.q: Which description fits broadband in the cabling comparison?
notesQuestions.answer: Different frequency channels carry simultaneous signals.
options: Different frequency channels carry simultaneous signals.
Only one undivided baseband channel is used.
Signals must be carried through glass.
Every signal must use a separate physical cable.
notesQuestions.explain: In this traditional cabling comparison, broadband divides the available frequency range into separate channels. Different channels can carry signals simultaneously rather than all users taking turns in one channel.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Here broadband refers to frequency-channel sharing, not just the everyday phrase fast Internet.

notesQuestions.q: Which statement about multimode fiber is correct?
notesQuestions.answer: It may use LEDs or lasers, depending on the technology.
options: It may use LEDs or lasers, depending on the technology.
It always uses only LEDs.
It always has a smaller core than single-mode fiber.
Its reach never depends on the transceiver.
notesQuestions.explain: Different modes can take different paths and arrival times, spreading a pulse. The larger core supports these modes, and the optics and fiber grade determine usable reach.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: A larger core allows multiple modes, whose different arrival times can spread a pulse.

notesQuestions.q: Which two properties does QAM vary together?
options: Amplitude and phase
Frequency and cable length
Phase and core diameter
Amplitude and IP prefix
notesQuestions.explain: Combining amplitude and phase creates multiple distinguishable symbol states. More states can carry more bits per symbol, but closer states require cleaner reception.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Amplitude is strength; phase is position relative to a reference wave. QAM varies both.

notesQuestions.q: In C = B × log₂(1 + S/N), what does B represent?
options: Channel bandwidth in hertz
Number of bytes in a frame
Signal power divided by noise power
Channel capacity in bits per second
notesQuestions.explain: Shannon’s B is the width of the available frequency band, measured in hertz. Multiplying it by log₂(1 + S/N) produces the theoretical capacity C in bits per second.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: B is the frequency space available; C is the resulting theoretical data-rate limit. They have different units.

notesQuestions.q: With bandwidth held constant, a higher signal-to-noise ratio does what to Shannon capacity?
options: Increases it
Always reduces it
Leaves it unchanged
Makes it exactly equal to the frame size
notesQuestions.explain: With B fixed, increasing S/N increases 1 + S/N and therefore its logarithm. The theoretical capacity C rises because a cleaner signal allows information states to be distinguished more reliably.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Keep bandwidth fixed and improve signal relative to noise: the theoretical limit goes up, not necessarily the actual application speed.

notesQuestions.q: Which unit does the Data Link layer organize for local delivery?
options: Frame
TCP segment
Application message
Routing-table entry
notesQuestions.explain: A local-link receiver needs addressing and error-check information around the carried data. That header/payload/trailer unit is the frame.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: The local wrapper is a frame; the IP wrapper inside it is a packet.

notesQuestions.q: Where is CSMA/CD needed?
options: Shared half-duplex Ethernet
