Ordinary full-duplex switched Ethernet
Every fiber link regardless of duplex
Every IP router regardless of link type
notesQuestions.explain: CSMA/CD solves simultaneous transmissions on a shared half-duplex Ethernet medium. A switched full-duplex link has separate simultaneous send/receive operation, so this collision procedure is unnecessary.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Look for shared and half-duplex before choosing collision detection.

notesQuestions.q: What does a passing Ethernet FCS check mean?
notesQuestions.answer: No corruption was detected by that check.
options: No corruption was detected by that check.
Every possible error has been ruled out.
The destination application has processed the data.
The routing table is correct.
notesQuestions.explain: The receiver recomputes the CRC and compares it with the received FCS. A match means that check detected no corruption; some error patterns can go undetected, so it is not proof that every bit is correct.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: An error detector can fail to detect an error. Passing is not the same as repairing or guaranteeing.

notesQuestions.q: What is binary 10101101 in decimal?
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: A 1 includes its place value; a 0 skips it. Do not count the number of 1s.

notesQuestions.q: A switch has not learned a unicast destination. What normally happens?
notesQuestions.answer: It floods the frame to other eligible ports in the same VLAN.
options: It floods the frame to other eligible ports in the same VLAN.
It forwards only to a known destination port anyway.
It sends the frame only back to the incoming port.
It changes the destination into its own MAC address.
notesQuestions.explain: Without a destination entry, the switch cannot choose one correct output port. It floods eligible ports in that VLAN except the incoming port, so the destination has a chance to receive the frame.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: The frame is still addressed to one recipient. Flooding an unknown unicast does not turn it into a broadcast address.

notesQuestions.q: Why use both IP and MAC addresses?
notesQuestions.answer: They support different scopes: routing across networks and local-link delivery.
options: They support different scopes: routing across networks and local-link delivery.
Both describe a device’s geographic street address.
Both are permanently fixed to the network card.
MAC addresses replace the need for network prefixes.
notesQuestions.explain: MAC identifies the next local frame delivery; IP gives routers a destination across networks. Routers can replace local frames along the path without requiring the application to choose every link address.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: IP is the routed destination; MAC is the local delivery label.

notesQuestions.q: How many host bits are left in an IPv4 /17 prefix?
notesQuestions.explain: IPv4 has 32 bit positions. /17 reserves the first 17 for the network. Subtract 32 − 17 = 15 remaining host bits. Counting address combinations would be the next step, 2¹⁵.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: The question asks for bits, not addresses. Stop after subtraction.

notesQuestions.q: How many times can :: appear in one IPv6 address?
options: Once
Twice
Once per hextet
Any number of times
notesQuestions.explain: The receiver counts the written groups and fills the remaining positions with zeros. Two separate double colons would not say how to divide the missing groups.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Count the written groups; the one missing stretch fills the count back up to eight.

notesQuestions.q: What should you infer from a missing traceroute hop response?
notesQuestions.answer: The router might not reply; the result alone does not prove a broken path.
options: The router might not reply; the result alone does not prove a broken path.
The destination must be offline.
The router must have no IP address.
Every later router must be unreachable.
notesQuestions.explain: Traceroute depends on routers replying to probes. A router may filter or limit those replies while continuing to forward normal traffic, so a missing reply alone cannot prove a broken path.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Silence in a diagnostic test is evidence to investigate, not a guaranteed outage.

notesQuestions.q: Which decision belongs primarily to physical network design?
notesQuestions.answer: Choosing specific switch hardware and cable types
options: Choosing specific switch hardware and cable types
Defining user needs before planning
Deciding the logical subnet organization alone
Defining application traffic requirements alone
notesQuestions.explain: The abstract connectivity plan must become actual equipment, media and placement. These installable choices form the physical design.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Choosing a cable or placing a switch is physical design; assigning subnet ranges is logical design.

notesQuestions.q: What is the demarcation point?
notesQuestions.answer: The boundary between the provider’s network and the customer’s network
options: The boundary between the provider’s network and the customer’s network
Every work-area wall socket
The last byte of an Ethernet frame
The boundary between host and network bits
notesQuestions.explain: The service connection crosses a responsibility boundary between provider and customer. Identifying that point helps determine which side must investigate or repair a problem.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Demarcation is a boundary of responsibility, not automatically a firewall or a router.

notesQuestions.q: How do MDF and IDF commonly relate?
notesQuestions.answer: The main distribution point connects secondary distribution areas.
options: The main distribution point connects secondary distribution areas.
Each IDF must be an Internet registry.
An MDF is a MAC-address field inside an IDF.
They are names for two different modulation methods.
notesQuestions.explain: An MDF is the main distribution location. IDFs serve additional areas and link back through backbone cabling, reducing the need to run every work-area cable to one faraway room.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Main location → backbone → intermediate location → nearby work areas.

notesQuestions.q: In a leaf-spine design, each leaf connects to which switches?
options: Every spine in that fabric
Only one other leaf
Only the physically nearest spine
Every end user without any spine connection
notesQuestions.explain: Each leaf connects to every spine, allowing traffic between leaves through available spines. This creates predictable paths and alternatives if a path fails.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Servers attach to leaves; leaves reach spines. Do not substitute campus core/distribution/access tiers for this pattern.

notesQuestions.q: Which SNMP operation asks for a managed-object value?
options: GET
SET
An Ethernet FCS check
A spanning-tree port block
notesQuestions.explain: A GET request names a managed object whose value the manager wants to read. The device agent returns the result if supported and permitted; GET does not request a configuration change.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: GET reads; SET requests a change; a trap reports an event.

notesQuestions.q: What does an authorized SNMP SET request do?
notesQuestions.answer: Requests a change to a supported writable managed object
options: Requests a change to a supported writable managed object
Reads a value without requesting any change
Replaces every device’s MIB definitions
Always reboots every router
notesQuestions.explain: A SET request asks the agent to assign a value to a writable managed object. The agent checks support, permissions and validity before accepting it, so not every value can be changed.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Being able to read a gauge does not imply permission to change its setting.

notesQuestions.q: Which description fits IETF working-group decisions?
notesQuestions.answer: Rough consensus developed through discussion and review
options: Rough consensus developed through discussion and review
Always a simple majority vote of all Internet users
One vendor chooses without review
Every proposal becomes a standard immediately
notesQuestions.explain: IETF working groups use rough consensus: participants discuss technical issues and address substantial objections. It is not simply a majority vote or an instruction from one vendor.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: These are people reviewing technical proposals. The goal is broad technical agreement, not counting devices or votes.

notesQuestions.q: Convert 10101101 from binary → decimal.
notesQuestions.explain:
A bit is one binary digit: either 0 or 1. In an eight-bit number, the positions are worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 from left to right. Start at 1 on the RIGHT and double each time you move left. These values are fixed; do not rearrange them.

Example: 10101101.
Place values: 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1
Binary digits:     1 |  0 |  1 |  0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1
A 1 means “include this value.” A 0 means “skip this value.” Think of each digit as an on/off switch for the value above it.

For 10101101, include 128, skip 64, include 32, skip 16, include 8, include 4, skip 2, include 1.
128 + 32 = 160
160 + 8 = 168
168 + 4 = 172
172 + 1 = 173
So 10101101 in binary is 173 in decimal. Do not count the 1s; add their POSITION values.

00000101 means 4 + 1 = 5. The zeros at the beginning do not add anything. That is why 101 and 00000101 have the same value. In networking we often keep all eight bits to show one byte clearly.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Line up the place values. Add a value only where the bit is 1.

notesQuestions.q: Convert 173 from decimal → binary.
notesQuestions.explain:
Start with a remaining amount of 173. Move from the biggest position to the smallest. If its value fits in the remaining amount, write 1 and subtract it. If it is too big, write 0 and keep the remaining amount. Write one digit for EVERY position.

128 fits in 173 → write 1; 173 − 128 = 45 left.
64 is too big for 45 → write 0; still 45 left.
32 fits in 45 → write 1; 45 − 32 = 13 left.
16 is too big for 13 → write 0; still 13 left.
So far: 1010.

8 fits in 13 → write 1; 13 − 8 = 5 left.
4 fits in 5 → write 1; 5 − 4 = 1 left.
2 is too big for 1 → write 0; still 1 left.
1 fits in 1 → write 1; 1 − 1 = 0 left.
Last four digits: 1101. Together: 10101101.

Read the 1 positions back: 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173. You got the starting number back, so your conversion works. If the remaining amount reaches zero early, fill every remaining position with 0.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Work from largest value to smallest. If it fits, write 1 and subtract; otherwise write 0.

notesQuestions.q: Convert AF from hexadecimal → binary.
notesQuestions.explain:
Four binary positions have values 8, 4, 2, 1. They can represent 0 through 15, exactly the values of one hex digit. So EVERY hex digit becomes exactly four bits, including zeros at the beginning.

Example: AF. Take A by itself. A means 10.
8 fits in 10 → 1; 2 left.
4 is too big → 0.
2 fits → 1; 0 left.
1 does not fit → 0.
A becomes 1010.

F means 15. 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15, so all four positions are on: 1111.
A → 1010
F → 1111
Keep the original order and join: AF → 10101111. Do not add the two groups together.

For 05: 0 becomes 0000 and 5 becomes 0101. Join them to get 00000101. Writing 5 as just 101 would lose the four-bit grouping that makes hex easy to read.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Convert each hex digit into exactly four bits and join in the original order.

notesQuestions.q: Convert 10101111 from binary → hexadecimal.
options: AF
FA
AE
BF
notesQuestions.explain:
Inside every four-bit group, the values are 8, 4, 2, 1. Start over with those values for the next group. Do not use 128, 64, 32, 16 for the first group when converting directly to hex.

1010 uses the 8 position and the 2 position.
8 + 2 = 10.
Hex uses A for 10, so 1010 becomes A.
Remember the letter values: A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.

1111 uses all four positions.
8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 → F.
First group A, second group F: the answer is AF. Preserve the order; AF and FA are different numbers.

Add zeros to the LEFT until the leftmost group has four bits. Example: 101 becomes 0101 → 4 + 1 = 5 → hex 5. Adding zeros to the right would change the number, so only pad on the left.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Group bits into fours from the right; convert each group using 8, 4, 2, 1.

notesQuestions.q: Convert AF from hexadecimal → decimal.
notesQuestions.explain:
Example: AF. A means 10 and F means 15. Do not add 10 + 15 yet: the A is in the sixteens position, so its position matters.

A in the sixteens position: 10 × 16 = 160.
F in the ones position: 15 × 1 = 15.
160 + 15 = 175.
So AF in hex is 175 in decimal.

Hex 20 means 2 × 16 + 0 × 1 = 32 in decimal. It does NOT mean decimal twenty. Always check which number system the question names. You may also see hex written as 0x20; 0x is a label meaning hexadecimal.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Multiply each digit by its position value, then add. The rightmost positions are 1 and 16.

notesQuestions.q: Convert 175 from decimal → hexadecimal.
options: AF
FA
AD
A5
notesQuestions.explain:
Example: 175.
10 × 16 = 160 fits.
11 × 16 = 176 is too much.
So 175 contains 10 full groups of 16.
175 − 160 = 15 left over. This leftover is called the remainder.

The group count is 10 → A.
The remainder is 15 → F.
Write the group digit first, then the remainder digit: AF.
Check: 10 × 16 + 15 = 175.

Decimal 35 contains 2 groups of 16, with 3 left over: 35 − 32 = 3. So it becomes hex 23. For a full byte, decimal 5 is hex 05. You can also convert decimal → eight-bit binary → two four-bit groups → hex if that method feels easier.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: For a byte, find full groups of 16 and the leftover. Translate 10–15 into A–F.

notesQuestions.q: Your turn with a new number: convert 00101010 from binary to decimal.
notesQuestions.explain: The 1s are at 32, 8 and 2. Add 32 + 8 + 2 = 42. The leading zeros contribute nothing.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Line up the place values. Add a value only where the bit is 1.

notesQuestions.q: Your turn with a new number: convert 42 from decimal to binary.
notesQuestions.explain: 128 and 64 are too big: write 00. Use 32: 10 left. Skip 16. Use 8: 2 left. Skip 4. Use 2: 0 left. Skip 1. The eight digits are 00101010.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Work from largest value to smallest. If it fits, write 1 and subtract; otherwise write 0.

notesQuestions.q: Your turn with a new number: convert 2A from hex to binary.
notesQuestions.explain: 2 is 0010 using the 8, 4, 2, 1 positions. A means 10, which is 8 + 2, or 1010. Join the groups: 0010 1010.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Convert each hex digit into exactly four bits and join in the original order.

notesQuestions.q: Your turn with a new number: convert 00101010 from binary to hex.
options: 2A
A2
2B
notesQuestions.explain: Split from the right: 0010 | 1010. The first group is 2. The second is 8 + 2 = 10, written A in hex. Join them: 2A.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Group bits into fours from the right; convert each group using 8, 4, 2, 1.

notesQuestions.q: Your turn with a new number: convert 2A from hex to decimal.
notesQuestions.explain: 2 counts sixteens: 2 × 16 = 32. A counts ones: 10 × 1 = 10. Add 32 + 10 = 42.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Multiply each digit by its position value, then add. The rightmost positions are 1 and 16.

notesQuestions.q: Your turn with a new number: convert 42 from decimal to hex.
options: 2A
A2
2B
notesQuestions.explain: Two groups of 16 fit: 2 × 16 = 32. Subtract 42 − 32 = 10 left over. The group count gives 2 and the remainder 10 gives A. Answer: 2A.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: For a byte, find full groups of 16 and the leftover. Translate 10–15 into A–F.

notesQuestions.q: You need unique labels for 9 objects. What is the smallest bit count that works?
options: 4 bits
3 bits
9 bits
2 bits
notesQuestions.explain: Three bits give 2³ = 8 choices, one too few. Four bits give 2⁴ = 16 choices, enough for all 9 objects. Choose the smallest count that is sufficient.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: Count combinations with powers of 2. Do not subtract network and broadcast reservations from general-purpose labels.

notesQuestions.q: A laptop sends to a server on a different IP network. On the first Ethernet link, whose MAC is the destination?
options: The local router’s interface MAC
The remote server’s MAC
Every router’s MAC combined
The laptop’s own MAC
notesQuestions.explain: The laptop first needs to deliver the packet to a router reachable on its local link. The IP destination remains the remote server, while the Ethernet destination identifies that first local router.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: first identify whether the action is local switching, routing to another link, or address translation.

notesQuestions.q: With ordinary routing and no NAT, what changes when a router sends a packet onto the next Ethernet link?
notesQuestions.answer: The source and destination MAC labels for the new link
options: The source and destination MAC labels for the new link
The final destination IP becomes the router’s IP
The destination application port changes at every router
The application message must name every switch
notesQuestions.explain: The incoming frame has finished its local delivery. A new frame uses the outgoing router interface as source and the next-hop interface as destination; the IP endpoints normally remain the same.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: first identify whether the action is local switching, routing to another link, or address translation.

notesQuestions.q: A Layer-2 switch forwards a frame within the same LAN. Must it replace the source and destination MAC addresses with its own?
notesQuestions.answer: No; ordinary Layer-2 forwarding preserves those addresses
options: No; ordinary Layer-2 forwarding preserves those addresses
Yes; every physical cable segment requires the switch’s MAC
Yes; it replaces both MACs with the server’s IP
No; because switches forward only IP headers
notesQuestions.explain: The switch selects an outgoing port for the existing local delivery. This is different from a router removing one link wrapper and building another for a new IP link.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: first identify whether the action is local switching, routing to another link, or address translation.

notesQuestions.q: Why is “IP addresses and ports always stay unchanged” too strong?
notesQuestions.answer: NAT can translate addresses, and port translation can change ports
options: NAT can translate addresses, and port translation can change ports
Every Layer-2 switch changes TCP ports
Ethernet always removes IP addresses permanently
TTL is another name for the source TCP port
notesQuestions.explain: Ordinary routing preserves the endpoint addresses and ports in this example. Address/port translation is a separate function that can change them; even ordinary routers still update TTL or Hop Limit.
notesQuestions.remember: Remember: first identify whether the action is local switching, routing to another link, or address translation.

notes-big-picture.title: Following one message
notes-big-picture.context: A network lets devices exchange information. Sending a message needs several jobs: prepare the data, identify the receiving application, find the destination network, cross the next local link, and transmit signals.
notes-big-picture.analogy: Like a delivery service: the letter, recipient, route, local delivery vehicle and road each play a different part.
notes-big-picture.example: You open a web page. Application protocols request it; Transport communicates between processes; IP routes packets; Data Link carries local frames; Physical transmits signals.

notes-1-1.title: Why networking is divided into layers
notes-1-1.context: In Chapter 1, a layer means one set of responsibilities in communication. The layers work together through defined interfaces. This makes a large system easier to build and troubleshoot.
notes-1-1.analogy: A restaurant separates taking orders, cooking and delivery. A new delivery vehicle does not require rewriting the menu.
notes-1-1.example: A browser can still request the same page after you change from Wi-Fi to Ethernet. The local connection changes; the browser’s network service can remain the same.

notes-1-2.title: The five jobs in your TCP/IP model
notes-1-2.context: Your course uses five layers. Application supplies network services. Transport connects application processes. Network chooses routes using IP. Data Link handles a local frame. Physical carries bits as signals.
notes-1-2.analogy: Think of delivery instructions: what to send, which recipient process, which network, the next local delivery, and the physical journey.
notes-1-2.example: A packet crossing several routers needs IP routing. Each individual local link uses a frame and physical signals. The five-layer course model separates those jobs. A Transport port number identifies the receiving application endpoint; for example, HTTP commonly uses port 80.

notes-1-3.title: Why OSI has seven layers
notes-1-3.context: Chapter 1 compares two ways of organizing network functions. OSI has seven layers. Its Presentation layer handles representation, such as formatting and encryption; Session manages conversations. TCP/IP groups these upper responsibilities under Application.
notes-1-3.analogy: OSI gives three separate desks to application services, formatting and conversation management. TCP/IP groups those desks into one upper department.
notes-1-3.example: OSI top to bottom: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Your five-layer TCP/IP list omits separate Presentation and Session entries.

notes-1-4.title: Wrapping and unwrapping data
notes-1-4.context: Encapsulation means adding control information around data as it travels down the sending stack. Decapsulation removes that wrapping as the receiver processes it up the stack.
notes-1-4.analogy: A letter goes into an addressed envelope, then into a local delivery container. Each wrapper helps with a different part of delivery.
notes-1-4.example: A router takes a packet out of its incoming frame, updates forwarding-related IP information, then builds a frame for the next link. The IP header is not completely unchanged.

notes-1-5.title: Who writes the shared rules?
notes-1-5.context: In Chapter 1, network authorities are organizations with different jobs. IEEE develops Ethernet and Wi-Fi standards. IETF develops Internet protocol standards. ICANN coordinates naming, and IANA coordinates shared number and parameter registries. TIA develops commercial building-cabling standards. ITU is the United Nations agency for international telecommunications.
notes-1-5.analogy: People agree on road signs so drivers from different towns understand them. Standards help devices made by different companies understand one another.
notes-1-5.example: Choose the job first: Ethernet or Wi-Fi rules → IEEE. Internet protocol rules → IETF. Coordinating Internet names and numbers → ICANN. Global identifier registries → IANA. International telecommunications → ITU. Building cabling standards → TIA. These are organizations or coordinating functions, not devices forwarding your packets.

notes-2-1.title: Turning information into something that travels
notes-2-1.context: In Chapter 2, bits are the 0s and 1s that represent information. A signal is a physical change that carries those bits. The medium is the path: copper wire, optical fiber or radio through space.
notes-2-1.analogy: A spoken word is an idea carried by vibrations in air. Network data also needs a physical carrier.
notes-2-1.example: Copper uses electrical signals; fiber uses light; wireless uses radio. Choosing a medium means checking speed, distance, interference and cost.

notes-2-2.title: Choosing and understanding copper cable
notes-2-2.context: UTP means Unshielded Twisted Pair. Pairs of copper wires are twisted to reduce interference between signals. Cable categories describe performance requirements; distance and installation matter too.
notes-2-2.analogy: Two conversations in one room can interfere. Cable design helps a receiver distinguish its intended conversation.
notes-2-2.example: Common limits: Cat 5e supports 1 Gbps over 100 m; Cat 6a supports 10 Gbps over 100 m. Cat 8 supports 25/40 Gbps over shorter 30 m channels and is shielded. In the traditional cabling comparison, baseband uses an undivided signaling channel; broadband separates simultaneous signals into frequency channels.

notes-2-3.title: How fiber guides light
notes-2-3.context: Fiber carries light through a core surrounded by cladding. Total internal reflection keeps light guided in the core under the right conditions. Single-mode uses a smaller core; multimode allows multiple light paths.
notes-2-3.analogy: Imagine light following a carefully designed tunnel. Different paths can arrive at slightly different times, spreading a pulse.
notes-2-3.example: Single-mode core: about 9 µm, commonly for long links. Multimode core: 50 or 62.5 µm, commonly for shorter links. Reach depends on the optics and data rate, not just the name.

notes-2-4.title: How a wave carries different values
notes-2-4.context: Modulation changes a signal property to represent information. Amplitude is its strength; frequency is how often it repeats; phase is its position in a cycle. QAM changes amplitude and phase together.
notes-2-4.analogy: You could signal with a flashlight by changing its brightness or timing. The receiver needs to distinguish the changes.
notes-2-4.example: AM changes amplitude; FM changes frequency; PM changes phase. More QAM states can encode more bits per symbol, but closely spaced states are harder to distinguish in noise.

notes-2-5.title: Sharing a medium and understanding its limits
notes-2-5.context: Multiplexing lets several signals share one medium. FDM assigns frequency bands; TDM assigns time slots. Shannon’s formula relates theoretical capacity to channel bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio.
notes-2-5.analogy: FDM resembles different radio stations. TDM resembles people taking turns speaking into one microphone.
notes-2-5.example: For C = B × log₂(1 + S/N), if B = 1000 Hz and S/N = 3, then 1 + 3 = 4, log₂(4) = 2, and C = 2000 bits/s. S/N here is a linear ratio.

notes-3-1.title: Local delivery has its own wrapper
notes-3-1.context: In Chapter 3, Data Link handles communication over one local link. It organizes bits into a frame, uses link-layer addresses, manages access to the medium and detects errors.
notes-3-1.analogy: A local delivery label helps the next delivery step. It is different from the overall route across cities.
notes-3-1.example: An Ethernet frame includes destination and source MAC addresses, its payload and an error check. Physical sends the signals that carry the frame.

notes-3-2.title: Taking turns on shared Ethernet
notes-3-2.context: Older shared half-duplex Ethernet allows only one successful transmission at a time. CSMA/CD means listen first, transmit when idle, detect a collision, stop and back off randomly. Full-duplex switched Ethernet does not use collision detection.
notes-3-2.analogy: Two people start talking at once. They stop and wait different lengths of time so they do not immediately interrupt again.
notes-3-2.example: After a collision, devices send a jam signal and stop transmitting, then wait a random backoff interval before retrying.

notes-3-3.title: Reading an Ethernet frame
notes-3-3.context: A frame is a structured package with fields in a defined order. The addresses say who it is for and who sent it. The payload carries data. FCS is an error-detection value.
notes-3-3.analogy: An envelope has address fields and contents; the receiver needs to know which part is which.
notes-3-3.example: For an ordinary untagged maximum: 14-byte header + 1500-byte payload + 4-byte FCS = 1518 bytes. The 8-byte preamble/SFD is outside that total. A passing FCS check means no corruption was detected; it is not an absolute guarantee that every bit is correct.

notes-3-4.title: MAC addresses and number systems
notes-3-4.context: A traditional Ethernet MAC address is 48 bits, often written as six hexadecimal byte groups. Binary uses 0 and 1. Decimal uses 0–9. Hexadecimal uses 0–9 and A–F.
notes-3-4.analogy: Different number systems are different ways of writing the same quantity, like writing twelve versus 12.
notes-3-4.example: 10101101₂ has 1s at 128, 32, 8, 4 and 1: add them to get 173. For hex, 1010 = 10 = A and 1111 = 15 = F, so 1010 1111 = AF.

notes-3-5.title: Hubs, switches and network shapes
notes-3-5.context: A hub repeats incoming signals to other ports. A switch learns which MAC address is reachable through which port. Redundant switch links can create loops; STP blocks selected paths to prevent this.
notes-3-5.analogy: A hub resembles shouting to a room. A switch resembles a receptionist who knows which desk to contact; if it does not know, it asks more widely.
notes-3-5.example: Star has a central device; bus uses a shared cable; ring forms a circle; mesh has multiple interconnections. A switch floods unknown unicasts within the VLAN.

notes-4-1.title: Why a device needs IP as well as MAC
notes-4-1.context: Chapter 4 concerns delivery across interconnected networks. An IP address identifies a network location for routing. A MAC address identifies an interface for local-link delivery. Neither is a person’s street address.
notes-4-1.analogy: An overall destination gets the package to the right area; each local delivery stage needs its own instructions.
notes-4-1.example: When a router forwards to a new link, it builds a new local frame. Keeping local addressing separate lets the link technology change without redefining the whole IP system.

notes-4-2.title: A subnet is a group of addresses
notes-4-2.context: An IPv4 address has 32 bits grouped into four 8-bit octets. A subnet groups addresses that share a starting set of bits. The number after / says how many bits are this shared network prefix. The remaining bits vary within the group.
notes-4-2.analogy: Think of a street name shared by several houses and a house number that distinguishes them. The analogy helps explain shared versus varying parts.
notes-4-2.example: For /17: 8 bits in octet 1 + 8 in octet 2 + 1 in octet 3 = 17 network bits. There are 32 − 17 = 15 host bits. Use the decoder to build this one bit at a time.

notes-4-3.title: Reading IPv6 without getting lost
notes-4-3.context: IPv4 has 32 bits. IPv6 has 128 bits, normally eight groups of 16 bits written in hexadecimal. Leading zeros within a group can be omitted. One :: can stand for consecutive all-zero groups.
notes-4-3.analogy: The double colon is a space-saving placeholder. You must still be able to work out exactly how many groups it replaces.
notes-4-3.example: 2001:0db8:aaaa:0000:0000:0000:eeee:0001 becomes 2001:db8:aaaa::eeee:1. Five groups remain visible, so :: represents three zero groups.

notes-4-4.title: Routes, diagnostic tools and address registries
notes-4-4.context: Chapter 4 asks how packets find networks and who organizes public addresses. A router uses a routing table as a list of destination networks and forwarding directions. RIRs are organizations that register and distribute Internet-number resources in regions.
notes-4-4.analogy: A routing table is a signpost list. A registry is more like the office keeping address assignments organized; it is not a delivery vehicle.
notes-4-4.example: Allocation means giving an organization a block of addresses to manage or distribute. An ISP can receive a block and assign addresses to customers. RIR coordination helps prevent conflicting public allocations. For diagnostics, Ping asks for an echo reply, Traceroute explores successive hops, and Pathping measures loss and timing over time. A missing reply may be caused by filtering; it does not prove that traffic cannot pass.

notes-12-1.title: Design starts with the people using the network
notes-12-1.context: Chapter 12 is about planning a real organization’s network. First identify the end-users, applications, locations, traffic and security needs. Logical design plans the organization of the network. Physical design chooses actual equipment and cabling.
notes-12-1.analogy: Plan rooms and their purpose before buying the furniture. Otherwise you may buy equipment that does not fit the need.
notes-12-1.example: A school estimates student devices and application traffic, plans subnets and services, then selects switches and cables. Costs include maintenance and downtime, not just purchase price.

notes-12-2.title: How building wiring is organized
notes-12-2.context: Structured cabling organizes permanent wiring and connection points. The demarc is the provider/customer boundary. An MDF is a main distribution point; IDFs serve other areas. Horizontal cabling reaches work areas; backbone cabling joins telecommunications spaces.
notes-12-2.analogy: A main hallway connects smaller hallways, and those lead to rooms. This is an analogy for main distribution, intermediate areas and work-area connections.
notes-12-2.example: A desk connects through a wall outlet to a floor telecommunications room. Backbone cabling links that room to other distribution areas. A typical copper channel allows 90 m permanent cable plus 10 m patch cords.

notes-12-3.title: Where the campus Core layer fits
notes-12-3.context: In Chapter 12, Core means a role in a campus network design—not an OSI layer or the glass core of a fiber. The three campus roles are Access, Distribution and Core. Access connects users; Distribution groups access networks; Core links major network regions quickly and reliably.
notes-12-3.analogy: Access resembles neighborhood streets, Distribution resembles roads connecting neighborhoods, and Core resembles the main highway between larger areas.
notes-12-3.example: A campus has buildings A and B. Each has access switches for users and distribution switches for aggregation. Core connections carry traffic between those distribution areas. A data center uses another common design called leaf-spine: servers attach to leaf switches, and each leaf connects to every spine switch. This is different from the campus three-tier pattern.

notes-12-4.title: How an administrator checks devices remotely
notes-12-4.context: In Chapter 12, network maintenance means keeping service working. SNMP lets management software communicate with agents running on devices. A MIB describes the managed objects, such as an interface counter or temperature value.
notes-12-4.analogy: A manager asks a local assistant for a reading. A labeled form tells both of them what each field means.
notes-12-4.example: GET asks for a value. SET requests a change to an authorized writable object. The MIB is the definition of the objects, not a person doing the monitoring.

notes-12-5.title: Working groups are people making shared rules
notes-12-5.context: In Chapter 12, standards are written technical specifications that help products work together. A working group is a group of people—such as engineers and technical experts—who develop and review a specification. It is not a group of computers.
notes-12-5.analogy: People agree on the size and shape of a plug so independently made plugs and sockets can fit together.
notes-12-5.example: A group identifies a need, discusses requirements and proposals, revises a draft and seeks approval. IEEE uses ballots; IETF working groups seek rough consensus through discussion.

teach-convert-binary-decimal.title: Binary → decimal · from zero
teach-convert-binary-decimal.context: Chapter 3 uses binary and hexadecimal to understand MAC addresses. Chapter 4 uses binary for IP addresses. Decimal is the ordinary counting system you already use: 0, 1, 2 … 10 … 173. Binary writes the same quantities using only 0 and 1. Converting changes how we write a number, not its size.
teach-convert-binary-decimal.analogy: The quantity stays the same. Only the way we write it changes.
teach-convert-binary-decimal.example: 00000101 means 4 + 1 = 5. The zeros at the beginning do not add anything. That is why 101 and 00000101 have the same value. In networking we often keep all eight bits to show one byte clearly.

steps.title: Start with the names
steps.body: Chapter 3 uses binary and hexadecimal to understand MAC addresses. Chapter 4 uses binary for IP addresses. Decimal is the ordinary counting system you already use: 0, 1, 2 … 10 … 173. Binary writes the same quantities using only 0 and 1. Converting changes how we write a number, not its size.

steps.title: Each position has a value
steps.body: A bit is one binary digit: either 0 or 1. In an eight-bit number, the positions are worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 from left to right. Start at 1 on the RIGHT and double each time you move left. These values are fixed; do not rearrange them.

steps.title: Line up the digits
steps.body:
Example: 10101101.
Place values: 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1
Binary digits:     1 |  0 |  1 |  0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1
A 1 means “include this value.” A 0 means “skip this value.” Think of each digit as an on/off switch for the value above it.

steps.title: Add only the switched-on values
steps.body:
For 10101101, include 128, skip 64, include 32, skip 16, include 8, include 4, skip 2, include 1.
128 + 32 = 160
160 + 8 = 168
168 + 4 = 172
172 + 1 = 173
So 10101101 in binary is 173 in decimal. Do not count the 1s; add their POSITION values.

steps.title: One smaller example
steps.body: 00000101 means 4 + 1 = 5. The zeros at the beginning do not add anything. That is why 101 and 00000101 have the same value. In networking we often keep all eight bits to show one byte clearly.

teach-convert-decimal-binary.title: Decimal → binary · from zero
teach-convert-decimal-binary.context: We want to write the ordinary number 173 using only 0s and 1s. For a number from 0 through 255, use eight positions: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Think of picking value cards that add up to 173.
teach-convert-decimal-binary.analogy: The quantity stays the same. Only the way we write it changes.
teach-convert-decimal-binary.example: Read the 1 positions back: 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173. You got the starting number back, so your conversion works. If the remaining amount reaches zero early, fill every remaining position with 0.

steps.title: What are we trying to build?
steps.body: We want to write the ordinary number 173 using only 0s and 1s. For a number from 0 through 255, use eight positions: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Think of picking value cards that add up to 173.

steps.title: The rule: can this value fit?
steps.body: Start with a remaining amount of 173. Move from the biggest position to the smallest. If its value fits in the remaining amount, write 1 and subtract it. If it is too big, write 0 and keep the remaining amount. Write one digit for EVERY position.

steps.title: Build the first four digits
steps.body:
128 fits in 173 → write 1; 173 − 128 = 45 left.
64 is too big for 45 → write 0; still 45 left.
32 fits in 45 → write 1; 45 − 32 = 13 left.
16 is too big for 13 → write 0; still 13 left.
So far: 1010.

steps.title: Finish the last four digits
steps.body:
8 fits in 13 → write 1; 13 − 8 = 5 left.
4 fits in 5 → write 1; 5 − 4 = 1 left.
2 is too big for 1 → write 0; still 1 left.
1 fits in 1 → write 1; 1 − 1 = 0 left.
Last four digits: 1101. Together: 10101101.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.body: Read the 1 positions back: 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173. You got the starting number back, so your conversion works. If the remaining amount reaches zero early, fill every remaining position with 0.

teach-convert-hex-binary.title: Hexadecimal → binary · from zero
teach-convert-hex-binary.context: Hexadecimal, or hex, has 16 digit symbols. After 0–9 it uses A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. These letters are number digits here. MAC addresses use hex because it is shorter to read than a long string of bits.
teach-convert-hex-binary.analogy: The quantity stays the same. Only the way we write it changes.
teach-convert-hex-binary.example: For 05: 0 becomes 0000 and 5 becomes 0101. Join them to get 00000101. Writing 5 as just 101 would lose the four-bit grouping that makes hex easy to read.

steps.title: Why are there letters in a number?
steps.body: Hexadecimal, or hex, has 16 digit symbols. After 0–9 it uses A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. These letters are number digits here. MAC addresses use hex because it is shorter to read than a long string of bits.

steps.title: One hex digit becomes four bits
steps.body: Four binary positions have values 8, 4, 2, 1. They can represent 0 through 15, exactly the values of one hex digit. So EVERY hex digit becomes exactly four bits, including zeros at the beginning.

steps.title: Convert A first
steps.body:
Example: AF. Take A by itself. A means 10.
8 fits in 10 → 1; 2 left.
4 is too big → 0.
2 fits → 1; 0 left.
1 does not fit → 0.
A becomes 1010.

steps.title: Convert F, then join
steps.body:
F means 15. 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15, so all four positions are on: 1111.
A → 1010
F → 1111
Keep the original order and join: AF → 10101111. Do not add the two groups together.

steps.title: Keep all four bits for each digit
steps.body: For 05: 0 becomes 0000 and 5 becomes 0101. Join them to get 00000101. Writing 5 as just 101 would lose the four-bit grouping that makes hex easy to read.

teach-convert-binary-hex.title: Binary → hexadecimal · from zero
teach-convert-binary-hex.context: Hex is a shorter way to write binary. Start at the RIGHT and split the bits into groups of four. Example: 10101111 becomes 1010 | 1111. Each group becomes ONE hex digit.
teach-convert-binary-hex.analogy: The quantity stays the same. Only the way we write it changes.
teach-convert-binary-hex.example: Add zeros to the LEFT until the leftmost group has four bits. Example: 101 becomes 0101 → 4 + 1 = 5 → hex 5. Adding zeros to the right would change the number, so only pad on the left.

steps.title: Make groups of four
steps.body: Hex is a shorter way to write binary. Start at the RIGHT and split the bits into groups of four. Example: 10101111 becomes 1010 | 1111. Each group becomes ONE hex digit.

steps.title: Give each group its own values
steps.body: Inside every four-bit group, the values are 8, 4, 2, 1. Start over with those values for the next group. Do not use 128, 64, 32, 16 for the first group when converting directly to hex.

steps.title: Convert the first group
steps.body:
1010 uses the 8 position and the 2 position.
8 + 2 = 10.
Hex uses A for 10, so 1010 becomes A.
Remember the letter values: A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.

steps.title: Convert the second group and join
steps.body:
1111 uses all four positions.
8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 → F.
First group A, second group F: the answer is AF. Preserve the order; AF and FA are different numbers.

steps.title: What if there are fewer than four bits?
steps.body: Add zeros to the LEFT until the leftmost group has four bits. Example: 101 becomes 0101 → 4 + 1 = 5 → hex 5. Adding zeros to the right would change the number, so only pad on the left.

teach-convert-hex-decimal.title: Hexadecimal → decimal · from zero
teach-convert-hex-decimal.context: In decimal, 23 means 2 tens plus 3 ones. In a two-digit hex number, the left digit counts groups of SIXTEEN and the right digit counts ones. Hex place values from right to left are 1, 16, 256, 4096. Each step left multiplies the place value by 16.
teach-convert-hex-decimal.analogy: The quantity stays the same. Only the way we write it changes.
teach-convert-hex-decimal.example: Hex 20 means 2 × 16 + 0 × 1 = 32 in decimal. It does NOT mean decimal twenty. Always check which number system the question names. You may also see hex written as 0x20; 0x is a label meaning hexadecimal.

steps.title: Hex digits have positions too
steps.body: In decimal, 23 means 2 tens plus 3 ones. In a two-digit hex number, the left digit counts groups of SIXTEEN and the right digit counts ones. Hex place values from right to left are 1, 16, 256, 4096. Each step left multiplies the place value by 16.

steps.title: Translate letters into values
steps.body: Example: AF. A means 10 and F means 15. Do not add 10 + 15 yet: the A is in the sixteens position, so its position matters.

steps.title: Multiply by the position, then add
steps.body:
A in the sixteens position: 10 × 16 = 160.
F in the ones position: 15 × 1 = 15.
160 + 15 = 175.
So AF in hex is 175 in decimal.

steps.title: Try a number without letters
steps.body: Hex 20 means 2 × 16 + 0 × 1 = 32 in decimal. It does NOT mean decimal twenty. Always check which number system the question names. You may also see hex written as 0x20; 0x is a label meaning hexadecimal.

teach-convert-decimal-hex.title: Decimal → hexadecimal · from zero
teach-convert-decimal-hex.context: For the byte-sized values used here (0–255), ask: how many full groups of 16 fit in the decimal number, and how many ones are left over? The group count becomes the left hex digit. The leftover amount becomes the right digit.
teach-convert-decimal-hex.analogy: The quantity stays the same. Only the way we write it changes.
teach-convert-decimal-hex.example: Decimal 35 contains 2 groups of 16, with 3 left over: 35 − 32 = 3. So it becomes hex 23. For a full byte, decimal 5 is hex 05. You can also convert decimal → eight-bit binary → two four-bit groups → hex if that method feels easier.

steps.title: Use groups of sixteen
steps.body: For the byte-sized values used here (0–255), ask: how many full groups of 16 fit in the decimal number, and how many ones are left over? The group count becomes the left hex digit. The leftover amount becomes the right digit.

steps.title: Find the full groups
steps.body:
Example: 175.
10 × 16 = 160 fits.
11 × 16 = 176 is too much.
So 175 contains 10 full groups of 16.
175 − 160 = 15 left over. This leftover is called the remainder.

steps.title: Turn both values into hex digits
steps.body:
The group count is 10 → A.
The remainder is 15 → F.
Write the group digit first, then the remainder digit: AF.
Check: 10 × 16 + 15 = 175.

steps.title: A smaller example and another route
steps.body: Decimal 35 contains 2 groups of 16, with 3 left over: 35 − 32 = 3. So it becomes hex 23. For a full byte, decimal 5 is hex 05. You can also convert decimal → eight-bit binary → two four-bit groups → hex if that method feels easier.

notes-number-labels.title: Bits, exponents & unique labels
notes-number-labels.context: Chapter 4 uses binary labels to give different objects different identifiers. Count how many choices the bits can make; this question does not ask how IP and MAC addresses route a packet.
notes-number-labels.analogy: One on/off switch has two choices. Two switches have four combinations. A third switch doubles that to eight.
notes-number-labels.example: For 10 bits, multiply ten factors of 2 to get 1,024 labels. For 200 objects, 128 choices are too few but 256 work, so 8 bits are enough.

notes-hop-delivery.title: Hop-by-hop vs. end-to-end delivery
notes-hop-delivery.context: Chapter 3 explains local frames; Chapter 4 explains IP delivery across networks; Chapter 1 places Transport above IP. Imagine sending a package through several delivery stops. The final destination stays on the inner address label, while each local handoff needs its own outer label.
notes-hop-delivery.analogy: The inner destination label stays with the package; each local delivery service adds its own next-stop label.
notes-hop-delivery.example: Assume Ethernet links and ordinary routing with no NAT. Laptop → Router A → Router B → Server. Each routed link uses a different source/destination MAC pair. The source/destination IP addresses still identify the laptop and server. TCP/UDP ports identify their application endpoints. Click each link in the diagram to see which labels change.

steps.title: One journey, two delivery scopes
steps.body: Chapter 3 explains local frames; Chapter 4 explains IP delivery across networks; Chapter 1 places Transport above IP. Imagine sending a package through several delivery stops. The final destination stays on the inner address label, while each local handoff needs its own outer label.

steps.title: What does “link-layer wrapper” actually mean?
steps.body:
Start with the message you want to send, such as a request for a web page. Your computer prepares an IP packet: a bundle of data that includes the final destination’s IP address.

To carry that packet across a local Ethernet connection, the computer adds information BEFORE it and AFTER it. Think of putting a letter into an envelope. This is only a picture to help you remember: the real envelope is extra bits, not paper.

HEADER = information before the packet. For Ethernet, it includes the source MAC (who sent this local frame), destination MAC (who receives this local frame), and type (what kind of packet is inside).

PAYLOAD = what is inside. In this example, it is the whole IP packet.

TRAILER = information after the packet. Ethernet puts the FCS error check here, helping the receiver detect damage.

FRAME = the whole thing: header + packet inside + trailer. “Link-layer wrapper” means that outer delivery information around the packet. It is another way of describing what the Data Link layer adds.

steps.title: Local-link delivery: the outer frame
steps.body: On an Ethernet link, the frame has source and destination MAC addresses. For a remote server, your laptop first addresses the frame to its local router, not to the remote server’s MAC address. A local switch can forward that frame without changing its source and destination MAC addresses.

steps.title: At the router: open one envelope, make the next
steps.body:
Imagine your laptop sending a letter to a faraway server. The IP packet inside names that server as the final destination. The first Ethernet envelope is addressed to your local router because that is the next place the laptop can deliver it.

The router receives the frame, checks and removes its local delivery information, and reads the IP destination to choose the next connection. This is what “removes the link-layer wrapper” means: open the current local-delivery envelope and take out the packet.

The router then builds the next link’s frame. On Ethernet, it adds a new header and error-check trailer. The new source MAC belongs to the router’s outgoing interface; the new destination MAC belongs to the next receiver.

The final server is still the IP destination in this example. The outer local label changes because the next delivery stop changes. Assume no NAT here. Other link technologies may use a different frame format.

steps.title: Follow the same message across three links
steps.body: Assume Ethernet links and ordinary routing with no NAT. Laptop → Router A → Router B → Server. Each routed link uses a different source/destination MAC pair. The source/destination IP addresses still identify the laptop and server. TCP/UDP ports identify their application endpoints. Click each link in the diagram to see which labels change.

steps.title: What end-to-end does—and does not—mean
steps.body: Transport is process-to-process: it connects application endpoints. IP supplies addressing across networks, but routers still make hop-by-hop forwarding decisions. “Same endpoints” does not mean the whole IP header stays unchanged: routers reduce TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6). NAT may translate IP addresses and, with port translation, ports. For the basic example, assume no NAT.

steps.title: Keep the scope straight
steps.body: A switch forwarding within one LAN is not the same as a router forwarding onto another IP link. In this lesson, hop-by-hop means local delivery between successive IP forwarding endpoints, not necessarily every physical cable segment. Remember: local MAC label for this leg, IP destination for the wider journey, port for the receiving program.

Layering.why: A browser can keep requesting pages after you switch from Ethernet to Wi-Fi because the lower-layer delivery details can change without changing the web request format.
Layering.hint: Remember: Think of dividing a group project into jobs: each person can improve their part without rewriting everyone else's work.

Protocol.why: Two devices must agree on message format and meaning. If one sends a request the other cannot interpret, a working cable alone cannot make them communicate.
Protocol.hint: Remember: A shared language needs rules about what each message means and how to reply.

TCP/IP.why: TCP handles an ordered conversation between programs; IP handles packet addressing across networks. The suite also includes other protocols, so these two names label a larger family.
TCP/IP.hint: Remember: Split the name into two jobs: TCP handles the conversation; IP handles where packets go.

Application layer.why: HTTP gives a browser and web server rules for requests and replies. Those services are close to the program's purpose, while lower layers handle delivery.
Application layer.hint: Remember: Ask what the program wants to do, such as request a page, rather than how a cable carries it.

Transport layer.why: One computer may run a browser and a mail app together. Transport ports distinguish the application endpoints so incoming data reaches the appropriate conversation.
Transport layer.hint: Remember: The destination computer is like a building; the port helps identify which office should receive the data.

Network layer.why: A destination can be several networks away. Routers read the destination IP address and choose a next hop, which explains why addressing and routing belong together here.
Network layer.hint: Remember: A local switch gets you across one local link; IP routing gets you toward another network.

Data Link layer.why: An IP packet needs a local wrapper to cross a particular link. Ethernet adds MAC addresses and an error check to form that wrapper, called a frame.
Data Link layer.hint: Remember: Think of the next delivery stop. The frame's local address can change when a router sends the packet onward.

Physical layer.why: A bit is an idea, not something a receiver can directly sense. The sender represents bits using voltage, light or radio so the receiver can measure them.
Physical layer.hint: Remember: Copper carries electrical signals; fiber carries light; wireless uses radio.

OSI.why: A common seven-job reference helps people compare network designs and locate faults even when vendors build different products.
OSI.hint: Remember: OSI is a map of responsibilities, not seven physical boxes inside a computer.

Presentation layer.why: A receiver needs to interpret a sender's representation of data. The OSI Presentation role covers format translation and concepts such as compression and encryption.
Presentation layer.hint: Remember: Changing how information is represented is different from choosing the route it travels.

Session layer.why: A continuing exchange needs a way to begin, coordinate and end the conversation. OSI names this conversation-management responsibility separately.
Session layer.hint: Remember: Think of opening and closing a meeting, rather than carrying each envelope to the meeting room.

Encapsulation.why: Each delivery layer adds its own control information: transport ports, then IP addresses, then local-link information. The previous unit becomes the next wrapper's contents.
Encapsulation.hint: Remember: Put the message inside labeled envelopes, one job at a time.

Decapsulation.why: The receiver processes the outer delivery information before passing the remaining contents upward. This lets the application receive its message without treating Ethernet labels as application data.
Decapsulation.hint: Remember: Open the outside envelope first, then the envelope inside it.

IEEE.why: IEEE's 802 standards families include wired Ethernet and wireless LAN rules. Shared specifications let interfaces made by different vendors use the same link technology.
IEEE.hint: Remember: Associate IEEE with the local connection: Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

IETF.why: Internet protocols must work across networks made by many organizations. IETF participants develop shared technical specifications through an open standards process.
IETF.hint: Remember: Associate IETF with Internet conversations and delivery rules, such as TCP/IP and DNS.

LAN.why: A classroom's computers and printer can communicate through local switches without being a nationwide network. The limited geographic scope makes this a LAN.
LAN.hint: Remember: Local describes the area covered, not a particular cable brand.

WLAN.why: Wi-Fi devices exchange local traffic through radio rather than requiring a cable to each device. The network is still local in scope.
WLAN.hint: Remember: The W adds wireless to LAN; it does not turn the network into a wide-area network.

TCP.why: TCP tracks sequence numbers and acknowledgments, retransmitting when necessary and presenting bytes in order to the receiving application.
TCP.hint: Remember: A missing piece can be requested again; ordered delivery is a transport service, not something IP alone promises.

IP.why: IP packets carry source and destination addresses so routers can forward them toward another network. IP itself does not guarantee arrival or order.
IP.hint: Remember: An address helps find a route; it does not guarantee that the delivery succeeds.

DNS.why: People use readable names, while network software needs records such as an IP address. DNS queries obtain those records from a distributed naming system.
DNS.hint: Remember: DNS is like looking up a contact's number before calling; it is not the call itself.

HTTP.why: A browser sends a request for a resource, and a server responds with a status and content. HTTP defines the meaning and format of that exchange.
HTTP.hint: Remember: Requesting a web page is an application job; forwarding its packets is a lower-layer job.

Interoperability.why: A computer and switch from different vendors can communicate when both implement compatible rules. Matching the shared specification matters more than matching the logo.

Physical medium.why: A signal needs somewhere to travel. Copper, optical fiber and radio space provide different paths with different distance and interference limits.
Physical medium.hint: Remember: Separate the path from the message: a cable is the medium; voltage changes are the signal.

Copper cable.why: Copper conductors allow electrical signal changes to travel between interfaces. Noise and signal loss affect how well the receiver can distinguish the changes.
Copper cable.hint: Remember: Electrical signals use the metal; a fiber link uses light instead.

Fiber-optic cable.why: A transmitter launches light into fiber and a receiver detects it. Because information is carried optically, electromagnetic interference does not induce electrical noise in the glass.
Fiber-optic cable.hint: Remember: Think light through glass, not electricity through copper.

Wireless.why: An antenna sends and receives electromagnetic signals through space. A cable is not needed between the radio endpoints, but interference and obstacles still affect reception.
Wireless.hint: Remember: No wire does not mean no physical signal: the radio wave is real.

UTP.why: Pairs of copper conductors are twisted to help reduce unwanted coupling and interference. Unshielded means there is no metallic cable shielding around those pairs.
UTP.hint: Remember: Unshielded describes what is absent; twisted pair describes the two wires wound together.

EMI.why: A nearby electromagnetic source can disturb an electrical signal and make its intended values harder to detect. This is unwanted energy, not useful data.
EMI.hint: Remember: A nearby electrical disturbance can act like background chatter while you are trying to listen.

Crosstalk.why: A signal in one nearby pair can couple into another pair. Twisting and proper cable construction help limit that unwanted interaction.
Crosstalk.hint: Remember: Cross-talk is one channel leaking into its neighbor.

Bandwidth.why: In signal math, bandwidth is a frequency range measured in hertz. In everyday network discussion the word may refer to data capacity, so the units tell you which meaning applies.
Bandwidth.hint: Remember: Hz measures frequency range; bits per second measures data rate. Check the units first.

Bit rate.why: Counting how many bits are transmitted each second gives a data rate. A symbol may represent more than one bit, so bit rate is not always symbol rate.
Bit rate.hint: Remember: Bits per second counts information digits sent over time.

Gbps.why: The lower-case b means bits. Dividing a bit rate by eight gives a byte-rate equivalent before allowing for overhead and other limits.
Gbps.hint: Remember: Eight bits make one byte: 8 Gbps corresponds to 1 billion bytes per second before overhead.

Noise.why: Random unwanted changes can make one intended signal value look like another. A receiver needs enough separation between valid signal states to tell them apart.
Noise.hint: Remember: Noise adds confusion; it is not the gradual weakening called attenuation.

Attenuation.why: Signals lose strength as they travel. If a signal becomes too weak relative to noise, the receiver may no longer distinguish the intended values.
Attenuation.hint: Remember: A voice becoming quieter with distance is the memory aid for signal loss.

Cat 5e.why: The category specifies cable performance, while Ethernet standards determine supported links. A properly installed Cat 5e channel commonly supports gigabit Ethernet to 100 m.
Cat 5e.hint: Remember: Remember the pair of limits together: 1 Gbps and a 100 m channel for this common use.

Cat 6.why: Cat 6 supports gigabit Ethernet to 100 m, but 10-gigabit operation has shorter distance limits that depend on installation conditions.
Cat 6.hint: Remember: A cable can support a faster speed only over a shorter distance; category alone is not the whole answer.

Cat 6a.why: The augmented category improves performance for 10GBASE-T over a full 100 m channel when properly installed.
Cat 6a.hint: Remember: The a is useful to associate with the full-distance 10-gigabit option.

Cat 8.why: Cat 8 uses shielding and supports short 25/40-gigabit copper channels up to 30 m. Calling it unshielded or assigning it the usual 100 m reach would miss its key limits.
Cat 8.hint: Remember: Fast, shielded, short: keep speed, shielding and distance together.

Total internal reflection.why: At a suitable angle, light traveling in the higher-index core reflects at the lower-index cladding boundary instead of escaping. That helps guide it along the fiber.
Total internal reflection.hint: Remember: The angle and the two materials matter; not every ray hitting any surface stays inside.

Core.why: In fiber, the central optical region guides the light. This is a material part of a cable, unrelated to the campus design tier also called Core.
Core.hint: Remember: First check context: fiber core carries light; campus core connects network regions.

Cladding.why: Its lower refractive index creates the boundary that helps confine light to the core. It is an optical part, unlike the outer protective jacket.
Cladding.hint: Remember: Core carries the light; cladding helps keep it guided; jacket protects the cable.

Single-mode fiber.why: A small core supports one spatial propagation mode, avoiding the multiple-path spreading associated with multimode fiber. Suitable optics make long links possible.
Single-mode fiber.hint: Remember: One mode means less spreading from different paths, not an automatic fixed distance for every link.

Multimode fiber.why: Different modes can take different paths and arrival times, spreading a pulse. The larger core supports these modes, and the optics and fiber grade determine usable reach.
Multimode fiber.hint: Remember: Multiple paths can blur pulses over distance; that is why reach is not unlimited.

Amplitude.why: Amplitude describes how far a signal moves from its reference level. Raising a wave's height changes amplitude without necessarily changing its cycles per second.
Amplitude.hint: Remember: Height or strength is amplitude; how often it repeats is frequency.

Frequency.why: If a wave repeats more cycles each second, its frequency increases. Hertz means cycles per second, not bits per second.
Frequency.hint: Remember: Count repeats in one second, not how tall each wave is.

Phase.why: Two waves can have the same height and frequency but be shifted relative to each other. That relative position within the cycle is phase.
Phase.hint: Remember: Imagine two equally fast runners at different positions on the same circular track.

Modulation.why: A carrier is varied in a controlled way so its states represent information. The receiver detects those changes to recover the encoded information.
Modulation.hint: Remember: The message tells the sender how to change the carrier.

AM.why: Information is represented by amplitude changes. Unwanted amplitude changes can therefore imitate part of the message and cause confusion.
AM.hint: Remember: For AM, watch the wave's height.

FM.why: Information is represented by changes in cycle rate. Amplitude disturbances are less directly confused with the encoded quantity, though performance depends on the system.
FM.hint: Remember: For FM, watch how closely the cycles are spaced.

PM.why: Information is represented by shifts in the carrier's phase relative to a reference. A phase shift differs from simply making the wave taller.
PM.hint: Remember: For PM, watch the position of the cycle compared with the reference.

QAM.why: Combining amplitude and phase creates multiple distinguishable symbol states. More states can carry more bits per symbol, but closer states require cleaner reception.
QAM.hint: Remember: More choices per symbol give more information, but make neighboring choices easier for noise to confuse.

Multiplexing.why: Several streams share a resource by separating their use, such as into frequency bands or time slots. They do not each need a dedicated physical cable.
Multiplexing.hint: Remember: One road can serve several travelers if there is a rule for sharing it.

FDM.why: Separate frequency bands let streams occupy the same medium simultaneously. A receiver selects the appropriate band, like tuning a radio station.
FDM.hint: Remember: Different frequency spaces at the same time.

TDM.why: Streams use assigned time intervals on the same resource. Taking turns separates them even when the same frequency range is reused.
TDM.hint: Remember: Different turns on the same resource.

Ethernet.why: Ethernet defines wired link behavior including frames and MAC addressing. IP can be carried inside Ethernet, but Ethernet and IP solve different delivery jobs.
Ethernet.hint: Remember: Ethernet handles the local link; IP handles network addressing beyond it.

Frame.why: A local-link receiver needs addressing and error-check information around the carried data. That header/payload/trailer unit is the frame.
Frame.hint: Remember: An IP packet can be the contents of an Ethernet frame.

Packet.why: IP adds a network-layer header around the transport data. A link then carries this whole unit as its payload.
Packet.hint: Remember: Packet is the IP wrapper; frame is the local-link wrapper outside it.

Payload.why: What counts as payload depends on which wrapper you are discussing. A full IP packet is Ethernet payload, including the IP header.
Payload.hint: Remember: Ask: contents of which wrapper?

NIC.why: A host needs an interface that can transmit and receive using the link technology. The NIC provides that connection rather than choosing Internet routes for every remote network.
NIC.hint: Remember: NIC is the computer's network doorway, not the entire network.

MAC.why: Media Access Control concerns local link access and addressing. An Ethernet MAC address identifies an interface for local frame delivery.
MAC.hint: Remember: MAC tells the local frame where to go; IP serves the wider routed journey.

OUI.why: In a traditional universally assigned MAC address, the first three byte pairs identify an IEEE-assigned organization prefix. The remaining part is assigned within that block.
OUI.hint: Remember: Three bytes × eight bits = 24 bits. Locally assigned MAC addresses need not identify a manufacturer.

Broadcast.why: One local message may need to reach everyone in a broadcast domain, for example during discovery. Routers normally stop Ethernet broadcasts from spreading into other networks.
Broadcast.hint: Remember: Everyone locally is different from everyone on the Internet.

Unicast.why: The destination identifies one recipient rather than a group. A switch with a known destination mapping can choose that recipient's port.
Unicast.hint: Remember: One addressed recipient is unicast, even if an unknown-destination frame is temporarily flooded.

CSMA/CD.why: On shared half-duplex Ethernet, simultaneous starts can collide even after listening. Detecting a collision and waiting different random times lets devices retry.
CSMA/CD.hint: Remember: Listen, send, detect collision, stop, wait randomly, retry. Full-duplex switched links do not use this collision procedure.

Collision.why: Two transmissions overlap on a shared half-duplex medium, preventing successful reception. Each sender must retry according to the access rules.
Collision.hint: Remember: Both devices tried to speak over the same shared path at once.

Backoff.why: If both senders retried after the same delay, they could collide again. Randomized waits reduce the chance of synchronized retries.
Backoff.hint: Remember: Different waiting times help break the tie.

Full duplex.why: Separate sending and receiving paths allow both endpoints to transmit at once. This removes the shared-medium collision situation in switched Ethernet.
Full duplex.hint: Remember: A two-way road with separate lanes allows simultaneous travel.

Half duplex.why: Both directions are supported, but the shared resource cannot carry both transmissions simultaneously without conflict.
Half duplex.hint: Remember: A walkie-talkie can talk both ways, but users take turns.

Preamble.why: A known alternating pattern helps the receiver synchronize before the frame begins. It is not a destination address or application payload.
Preamble.hint: Remember: Get the receiver ready first; then mark where the actual frame starts.

SFD.why: After synchronization, a distinct one-byte pattern marks the start boundary so the receiver knows where frame fields begin.
SFD.hint: Remember: Preamble prepares; delimiter marks the boundary.

Destination MAC.why: A switch uses the destination field to decide where a frame should go on the local network. Across a router, a new link frame uses the next local destination.
Destination MAC.hint: Remember: Destination answers who receives this local frame, not who originally created the application message.

Source MAC.why: Switches learn which MAC addresses are reachable through incoming ports by examining the source field.
Source MAC.hint: Remember: Source tells who sent this frame; destination tells where it should go.

EtherType.why: The receiver must know how to interpret the payload. EtherType says which protocol, such as IPv4 or IPv6, follows the Ethernet header.
EtherType.hint: Remember: This label says what is inside the envelope.

Padding.why: A short payload needs extra bytes so the Ethernet frame reaches its minimum size. Padding does not turn into additional meaningful application data.
Padding.hint: Remember: Fill unused space to reach the minimum frame length.

FCS.why: The sender computes a check value over the frame and includes it at the end. A receiver compares its own calculation to detect corruption.
FCS.hint: Remember: A mismatch signals damage; the check itself does not repair the data.

CRC.why: CRC is the calculation that produces a check value. FCS is the field carrying that value in an Ethernet frame.
CRC.hint: Remember: Calculation versus container: CRC computes it; FCS carries it.

MTU.why: An Ethernet IP MTU of 1500 counts the carried network-layer packet. Adding the Ethernet header and FCS makes a larger frame.
MTU.hint: Remember: 1500 is commonly the IP packet limit, not the entire 1518-byte untagged Ethernet frame.

Bit.why: One binary position has two possible values, so each additional bit doubles the number of possible combinations.
Bit.hint: Remember: One switch has two states; two switches have four combinations.

Byte.why: Grouping eight binary digits creates 2⁸ = 256 possible patterns. Network sizes in bytes therefore differ by a factor of eight from sizes in bits.
Byte.hint: Remember: Eight bits fit in one byte; do not confuse b with B.

Octet.why: The word explicitly means eight bits. Each dotted decimal IPv4 part represents one such eight-bit group.
Octet.hint: Remember: An IPv4 part can display 0 or 255 and still occupy the same eight bit positions.

Nibble.why: Four bits have 16 possible patterns, matching exactly the 16 hexadecimal digit values.
Nibble.hint: Remember: One hex digit is one nibble; two hex digits make a byte.

Binary.why: The position values double as you move left: 1, 2, 4, 8. Add only the values whose digit is 1.
Binary.hint: Remember: 1010 means 8 + 2, not the decimal number one thousand ten.

Decimal.why: Each position is ten times the one on its right. For example, 42 means four tens and two ones.
Decimal.hint: Remember: The familiar counting system is only one way to write a quantity.

Hexadecimal.why: Each position is sixteen times the one on its right. A through F provide single symbols for values 10 through 15.
Hexadecimal.hint: Remember: Hex 2A means two sixteens plus ten: 32 + 10 = 42.

Hub.why: A hub repeats a received signal without reading a learned destination table. Connected half-duplex devices share the same collision domain.
Hub.hint: Remember: A hub repeats; it does not choose a port by looking up a MAC address.

Switch.why: A switch learns from source MAC addresses and looks up destination MAC addresses when forwarding. Unknown unicast and broadcasts are flooded within their VLAN.
Switch.hint: Remember: Learn from source, forward by destination.

STP.why: Extra switch links provide alternatives but can also form forwarding loops. STP blocks selected paths so active forwarding remains loop-free.
STP.hint: Remember: Keep backup roads available without letting a frame circle forever.

Topology.why: A topology shows how devices and connections are arranged. Physical wiring and the logical flow of traffic may have different shapes.
Topology.hint: Remember: Look at which nodes connect, not merely where icons are drawn on the page.

Star topology.why: Each endpoint has its own link to a central device. That central connection pattern is the identifying feature.
Star topology.hint: Remember: Spokes meet at one center.

Bus topology.why: Multiple devices share a common main path. The shared backbone, rather than a separate center-to-endpoint link for each device, identifies a bus.
Bus topology.hint: Remember: Several stops along one shared line.

Ring topology.why: Each part connects along a loop that returns to its starting point. The circular connection structure identifies the ring.
Ring topology.hint: Remember: Follow the links and you come back around.

Mesh topology.why: Multiple interconnections create alternative paths. In a full mesh, every pair is directly connected; a partial mesh has fewer links.
Mesh topology.hint: Remember: Several ways through, not just one center or one line.

VLAN.why: A switch can separate ports into logical broadcast domains. Frames in one VLAN do not simply become local broadcasts in every other VLAN.
VLAN.hint: Remember: One physical switch can host several separate logical local networks.

Router.why: A router uses destination IP prefixes and forwarding information to move packets between networks. A basic Layer-2 switch instead forwards local frames by MAC address.
Router.hint: Remember: Use a router when the packet must leave its local IP network.

Routing.why: A forwarding decision chooses the next step toward a destination. Each router makes its own decision using its available routes.
Routing.hint: Remember: You do not have to know every street to choose the next useful turn.

Routing table.why: Entries associate destination prefixes with an outgoing interface or next hop. A router matches the packet's destination against these entries.
Routing table.hint: Remember: It is a list of where to send traffic for address ranges, not a complete drawing of every device.

Next hop.why: A packet may need several routers to reach its final destination. The next hop is just the immediately following forwarding stop.
Next hop.hint: Remember: Next stop and final destination are not necessarily the same place.

IPv4.why: Four groups of eight bits give 32 bits total. Decimal dots make the groups easier to read, but routers work with the bit values.
IPv4.hint: Remember: Four octets × eight bits; a slash prefix says how those bits are divided.

IPv6.why: Eight groups of sixteen bits give 128 bits. Hexadecimal provides a compact representation, and zero compression can shorten it further.
IPv6.hint: Remember: Colons separate groups; each full group has four hex digits, not four bits.

Network portion.why: The prefix identifies the subnet shared by its members. Two interfaces in that subnet can share those bits while differing in the remaining positions.
Network portion.hint: Remember: The common street portion of the address is the memory aid.

Host portion.why: The bits after the prefix can vary within the subnet. Their patterns create address choices, although ordinary IPv4 subnets reserve the all-zero and all-one patterns.
Host portion.hint: Remember: Host bits are positions; host addresses are the values formed from those positions.

CIDR.why: A variable prefix length lets the address block size match needs more closely than the old fixed classes. The slash number counts network bits.
CIDR.hint: Remember: A larger IPv4 prefix leaves fewer host bits and therefore a smaller block.

Prefix length.why: IPv4 contains 32 positions. Reserving 17 for the network leaves 15 for the host portion, so /17 is not a count of hosts.
Prefix length.hint: Remember: Subtract the slash number from 32 before counting addresses.

Subnet mask.why: Mask ones select the network portion and mask zeros identify the host portion. A /24 mask has 24 ones followed by eight zeros.
Subnet mask.hint: Remember: The mask marks positions; it is not the destination device's address.

Network address.why: Setting all host bits to zero gives the first address of an ordinary subnet. That value names the subnet rather than an individual host.
Network address.hint: Remember: For 192.168.5.34/24, keep the first three octets and zero the last: 192.168.5.0.

Broadcast address.why: Setting all host bits to one gives the final address of an ordinary IPv4 subnet. It is reserved for reaching the subnet rather than assigning it to one interface.
Broadcast address.hint: Remember: For /24, the final eight bits become 11111111, which is 255. /31 point-to-point and /32 have special rules.

Classful addressing.why: Fixed class sizes can force an organization to accept far more addresses than needed. CIDR varies the prefix instead of forcing those fixed sizes.
Classful addressing.hint: Remember: A choice of only a few huge box sizes wastes space; variable prefixes allow a closer fit.
